title: Spinning Wheels and Their Spread
text:
Spinning Wheels and Their Spread

Before the wheel, nearly all yarn was made with a spindle. The spinner drafted fibre by hand, let a weighted spindle twist it, and wound the finished thread onto the shaft. The method is portable and needs little equipment, and it remains in daily use in many regions, including parts of the Andes, Central Asia and the Middle East. The spinning wheel did not replace the spindle everywhere. It added a faster way of working, in which a rotating wheel drives the spindle or flyer while both of the spinner's hands stay free to manage the fibre.

Origins

The place and date of the first spinning wheel are uncertain, and scholars still debate the evidence. Many historians favour the Indian subcontinent, where a simple hand-cranked wheel seems to have been in use by the first millennium CE. Chinese texts and images show wheel-driven devices for twisting and winding bast fibres and silk, and it is not always clear whether these were true spinning wheels or related machines for reeling and doubling. Early evidence is sparse because wheels were made of wood and rarely survived, and pictures and written references are often ambiguous.

Movement Across Asia and Europe

From South Asia the wheel appears to have travelled west through the Islamic world along trade routes, and it is documented in Persian and Arabic sources of the medieval period. It reached Europe by the thirteenth century. Early European wheels were of the "great wheel" or "walking wheel" type. The wheel was large and was turned by hand while the spinner stepped back and forth to draw out the fibre. This design suited wool, and it is still used by some hand spinners today.

The wheel changed the organisation of textile work. Spinning was faster, so yarn supplied weavers more readily, and some medieval town regulations dealt with the new tool. Some of them restricted its use for particular kinds of thread, which suggests that guilds and authorities were concerned about the quality of the yarn it produced. Over time spinning with the wheel became widespread in households, where it was mostly women's work. The English word "spinster", which originally meant someone who spun, comes from this association.

The Flyer and the Treadle

The most important European development was the flyer, a U-shaped device fitted with hooks that twists the yarn and winds it onto a bobbin in one continuous action. A treadle, which frees both hands, was added to it. The resulting "Saxony wheel" appeared in the later medieval and early modern period. Tradition credits a single inventor in the early sixteenth century, but this is probably a simplification, and the flyer is more likely to have developed in stages. Later forms included upright and table-top wheels, such as the castle and the Scotch tension types. Regional designs developed to suit local fibres, spaces and habits, and Scandinavian, Irish, French and Canadian wheels each have distinctive features.

The Charkha and Cultural Meaning

In India the hand-cranked wheel, known as the charkha, kept its importance for much longer. A compact portable version, the box charkha, folds into a case and is easy to carry. In the early twentieth century Mohandas Gandhi made the charkha a symbol of self-reliance and of resistance to imported mill-made cloth. He encouraged people to spin their own yarn and wear hand-woven cotton known as khadi. A spinning wheel appeared on early versions of the Indian national flag, and the Ashoka wheel on the present flag is often said to recall it.

Mechanisation

From the later eighteenth century, machines such as the spinning jenny, the water frame and the mule moved spinning from homes to factories, and handspun yarn lost most of its commercial importance in industrialising countries. Hand spinning survived as a domestic craft, a form of rural livelihood and a means of producing special yarns. In the twentieth century and since, there has been renewed interest in it among hobbyists, small-scale wool producers and craft communities. Modern wheels are made in many designs, and some are electrically driven.

title: Backstrap Loom Weaving
text:
Backstrap Loom Weaving

The backstrap loom is among the oldest and most widely distributed weaving devices in the world. It is a portable, tension-based loom in which one end of the warp is fixed to a stationary object, such as a post, tree or wall, while the other end is attached to a bar that rests against the weaver's lower back. By leaning backward or moving the hips forward, the weaver tightens or loosens the warp threads, controlling tension directly with the body. Because the loom has no rigid frame, it can be rolled up and carried, and the cloth it produces is limited in width by the span of the weaver's arms rather than by the size of any fixed structure.

Distribution and History

Backstrap weaving is practised across a broad range of regions, including the highlands of the Andes, Mesoamerica, parts of Southeast Asia, southern China, and Japan's Ainu communities, where related forms were used. Archaeological evidence from the Americas, including woven fragments and spindle whorls, indicates that the technique was well established long before European contact. Ceramic figures from pre-Columbian sites in Peru and Mexico show women seated with looms of this kind, and depictions in Maya art link weaving closely to female deities and to social status. In Asia, similar looms appear in the traditions of upland peoples in Indonesia, the Philippines, Laos, Myanmar and Taiwan.

Structure and Operation

A typical backstrap loom consists of a small number of simple parts. Two beams hold the warp at either end. A shed stick and a heddle rod, often a slender piece of wood or cane, separate the warp threads into alternating layers so that the weft can be passed through. A flat sword-shaped beater, frequently made of hardwood or bone, is used to pack each weft pass tightly against the previous one. The weft is wound onto a stick or small bobbin and passed through the opening, or shed, by hand.

Since the warp is continuous and often wound in a loop, many textiles woven on these looms have finished edges on all four sides and little waste. Weavers commonly produce narrow panels that are later joined to make garments, or tubular cloth that can be used with minimal cutting.

Techniques and Patterning

Although the loom is simple, the range of patterning achievable on it is considerable. Plain weave is the foundation, but weavers also create warp-faced and weft-faced fabrics, in which either the warp or the weft dominates the surface. Complex-weave techniques include supplementary weft brocading, where extra threads are inserted by hand to form motifs, and warp pick-up, in which the weaver selects individual warp threads by hand to form raised designs. Double-cloth and twill structures are also found in some traditions.

Designs are usually memorised or learned through repeated practice rather than written down. Motifs may represent animals, plants, mountains, ancestors or cosmological ideas, and the arrangement of bands and colours can identify a specific village, family or ethnic group. In many Andean and Guatemalan communities, a garment's pattern allows others to recognise where the wearer comes from.

Materials and Dyeing

Common fibres include cotton, wool from sheep, alpaca and llama, bast fibres such as hemp and ramie, and silk in parts of Asia. Yarns are traditionally hand-spun with a drop spindle and coloured with natural dyes, including indigo, cochineal, madder and various barks and roots. Synthetic yarns and commercial dyes have since become widespread, though many weavers continue to use natural materials for ceremonial or high-value work.

Cultural Significance and Contemporary Practice

Backstrap weaving is often transmitted from mother to daughter and is bound up with identity, ritual and the economy of the household. Cloth may be used in clothing, burial offerings, marriage exchanges and religious ceremonies. In recent decades, cooperatives and non-governmental organisations have supported weavers in selling their work to wider markets, offering income while encouraging the preservation of traditional designs. At the same time, pressures such as cheaper factory-made cloth, migration and changing patterns of education have reduced the number of people who learn the craft, prompting documentation and revival efforts in many communities.

title: Warp-Weighted Looms
text:
Warp-Weighted Looms

The warp-weighted loom is one of the oldest known forms of loom and was used across a wide area of Europe, the Mediterranean, and western Asia from the Neolithic period onward. It is a vertical loom, usually leaning against a wall or set into a frame, in which the warp threads hang freely from a horizontal beam and are held taut by weights attached to their lower ends. The design is simple, but it allows weavers to produce plain cloth, twills, and elaborate patterned fabrics, and in some regions it remained in use well into the twentieth century.

Structure and operation

The loom consists of two upright posts supported at the top by a horizontal cloth beam. The warp threads are fastened to this beam and hang downward in groups. Each group is tied to a weight, commonly made of fired clay, unfired clay, or stone. The weights keep the threads under even tension and prevent them from tangling. Because the tension comes from gravity rather than from a second beam, the loom needs no mechanism for winding or locking the warp at the bottom.

Warp threads are usually divided into two layers, or sheds, one in front of the other. A heddle rod, which is a horizontal bar, is attached to selected threads by loops of string called leashes. When the weaver pulls the rod forward, the threads connected to it move in front of the others, opening a space through which the weft can be passed. A shed rod holds open the natural shed between the layers. Alternating the two positions produces the basic plain weave. In twill weaving, additional heddle rods are used so that the warp threads can be lifted in more complex sequences.

The weft is beaten upward rather than downward. The weaver pushes each pass of weft toward the top of the loom using a flat tool, often made of wood, bone, or antler, sometimes called a weaving sword or beater. As a result, the cloth grows from the top downward, and the finished fabric is gradually rolled or left hanging on the upper beam. This direction of work is a distinctive feature of the warp-weighted loom, and it influenced the way starting borders and finished edges were made.

Archaeological evidence

Much of what is known about the warp-weighted loom comes from loom weights found at settlement sites. Clay weights, often pierced and shaped like rings, discs, or truncated pyramids, appear in large quantities at many excavated houses. Their arrangement in rows on the floor, where a loom once collapsed or was burned, has allowed archaeologists to estimate the width and position of individual looms. Depictions on Greek painted pottery, including scenes that show women weaving, provide further information about how the loom was set up and used.

Differences in weight size and shape are often interpreted as evidence of different fabrics. Lighter weights suggest finer threads and thinner cloth, while heavier ones suggest coarse wool or thicker yarns. Researchers also study the wear on weights and the spacing between them to understand how the warp was arranged.

Regional traditions

In Scandinavia, the warp-weighted loom persisted for a very long time. In Iceland and parts of Norway it was used to make a heavy, twilled wool cloth, and in Iceland it was associated with the production of vaðmál, a plain or twill fabric that served as a standard of value in medieval trade. Medieval written sources and later folk practice indicate that the loom was often set up in a dedicated room or in the main dwelling during the winter months.

In the Mediterranean world, the loom is widely associated with the textile work of ancient Greece and Rome. Literary sources describe weaving as a household activity, and the loom appears in myth and poetry as a symbol of domestic skill. Similar looms were used in Anatolia, the Near East, and parts of central Europe. In Scandinavia and the Faroe Islands, some weavers have revived the technique in recent decades, often working from archaeological reconstructions.

Decline and revival

The warp-weighted loom was gradually replaced in most regions by the two-beam vertical loom and later by the horizontal treadle loom, which allowed longer cloth to be woven and was better suited to commercial production. Today the loom is used mainly by museums, experimental archaeologists, and craft practitioners who wish to reproduce historical textiles and to study how early fabrics were made.

title: Floor Looms and Treadle Weaving
text:
Floor Looms and Treadle Weaving

The floor loom is a large, freestanding frame loom operated by the weaver from a seated position, with the feet working treadles that raise and lower sets of warp threads. It is distinguished from backstrap, warp-weighted and other portable looms by its rigid structure, its mechanical shedding system, and its capacity to produce long lengths of cloth with consistent tension. Looms of this general type have been used across Asia, Europe, Africa and the Americas, and many regional variants remain in use among hand weavers today.

Structure and Operation

The basic frame supports a warp beam at the back, onto which the lengthwise threads are wound, and a cloth beam at the front, where the finished fabric is gathered. Between them, the warp passes through the heddles, small loops of cord, wire or metal that are mounted on frames called shafts or harnesses. Each warp thread is threaded through a heddle and then through a dent in the reed, a comb-like device that spaces the threads and is held in a swinging frame called the beater, or batten.

When the weaver presses a treadle, the attached shafts lift certain warp threads and leave others in place, opening a gap known as the shed. The weft is carried through the shed on a shuttle, and the beater is then pulled forward to press the new weft against the edge of the cloth. The treadle is released or changed, a different shed is formed, and the sequence repeats. Because the hands are free to throw the shuttle and manage the beater, the process is considerably faster than with looms that require the weaver to open each shed by hand.

The pattern of the weave is determined by how the warp threads are distributed among the shafts and by the order in which the treadles are connected to them, called the tie-up. Plain weave, twill, satin and many more complex structures can be produced by changing these arrangements. Looms with additional shafts allow greater variety, and those with a large number of shafts can be used for elaborate patterns such as diapers and damask-like figures.

Historical Development

Treadle-operated looms are generally thought to have appeared in Asia before spreading westward. Chinese textile production made use of foot-operated devices for lifting warp threads at an early date, and treadle looms were employed in silk weaving. In Europe, horizontal treadle looms became established in the medieval period and contributed to the growth of urban weaving trades and guilds. Their use shifted some cloth production from household settings into specialized workshops, a change that is documented in records from many towns.

Later developments included the flying shuttle, patented by John Kay in 1733, which allowed a single weaver to throw the shuttle across a wide cloth with a cord-and-picker mechanism. The Jacquard attachment, introduced in the early nineteenth century, controlled individual warp threads by means of punched cards and made figured weaving more efficient. Both inventions were adapted to power looms, but they also influenced hand-operated looms in workshops and homes.

Regional Traditions

In Scandinavia, counterbalance and countermarch looms became central to household weaving, and are associated with woven coverlets, tapestry-like textiles and striped household linens. In the Appalachian region of the United States, settlers wove coverlets and utilitarian cloth on heavy timber looms, often built by the weavers themselves. In West Africa, men traditionally weave narrow strips on horizontal treadle looms, and the strips are sewn together to make wide cloths such as kente in Ghana. In India, pit looms, in which the treadles are placed in a hollow dug into the floor, remain common in handloom communities producing cotton, silk and brocade. Japanese and Southeast Asian weavers likewise maintain loom forms suited to local fibres and cloth types.

Contemporary Practice

Today floor looms are used by professional craftspeople, cooperatives and hobbyists. Many weavers value them for their versatility, and revival efforts in several countries have sought to preserve regional techniques alongside modern design work.

title: Draw Looms and the Jacquard Mechanism
text:
Draw Looms and the Jacquard Mechanism

Draw looms are weaving devices designed to control individual warp threads, or small groups of them, so that complex figured patterns can be produced and repeated without rethreading the loom. They developed in several regions where patterned silk, linen and wool cloths were highly valued, and they represent one of the most significant steps toward mechanised pattern control in the history of textile production.

Principle of the draw loom

On an ordinary harness loom, the weaver raises and lowers warp threads in a limited number of fixed groups, each tied to a shaft. This restricts the design to simple geometric patterns. A draw loom adds a separate system of cords, often called the figure harness, that connects selected warp threads to a set of pulling cords gathered at the side or above the loom. By pulling a particular group of cords, the operator lifts exactly those warp threads that are needed to form one row of the design. The cords are arranged in a sequence that corresponds to the pattern, and the sequence can be repeated as often as required.

Because the pattern is stored in the arrangement of the cords, an elaborate design needs to be prepared only once. Setting up the cords is slow and demanding work, but after it is complete, long lengths of cloth with the same figured motif can be woven.

The drawboy and the weaver

In the traditional form of the loom, two people work together. The weaver sits at the front, passes the shuttle and operates the foot treadles, while a second worker, known as the drawboy or drawgirl, sits or stands beside or above the loom and pulls the cords in turn. The name reflects the fact that the helper was often a child or apprentice, although skilled adults also did this work. Coordination between the two is essential, since a single mistaken pull disturbs the design.

Regional traditions

Draw looms are associated with many weaving cultures. In China, large drawlooms were used for silk damasks, brocades and other figured fabrics, and workshops with such equipment supplied imperial and commercial markets. Knowledge of figured silk weaving spread along trade routes to Central Asia, Persia, the Byzantine world and eventually Italy, where cities developed prominent silk industries. In Japan, the tall loom used at Kyoto's Nishijin district for obi and ceremonial textiles follows a related principle. Draw looms were also used in South Asia, where figured silks and the elaborate brocades of centres such as Varanasi were produced, and in parts of Europe for damask table linen.

Toward mechanical control

As demand for figured silk increased in Europe, inventors sought ways to reduce the labour of the drawboy and the time spent preparing the cords. In the early eighteenth century, Basile Bouchon of Lyon devised a method of controlling the needles that selected warp threads by means of a perforated paper tape. Later workers, including Jean-Baptiste Falcon, replaced the tape with a chain of punched cards, and Jacques de Vaucanson experimented with automatic control of the loom.

The Jacquard mechanism

Joseph Marie Jacquard, a Lyon inventor, combined and refined these ideas in a device first shown in the early years of the nineteenth century. It was mounted above the loom. A series of rigid hooks, each linked to a warp thread or small group of threads, was either engaged or left aside according to the presence or absence of holes in a card. Each card corresponded to one pick of the weft. The cards were laced together in a continuous chain and advanced automatically as weaving proceeded, so a single operator could produce patterns that previously needed a helper.

The mechanism could be fitted to existing looms and permitted far larger and more detailed designs, including pictorial work. A well-known woven portrait of Jacquard, made in the 1830s from a very large set of cards, is often cited as a demonstration of the technique.

Social and technological effects

The device was adopted widely, though not without resistance. Lyon's silk weavers, the canuts, feared for their livelihoods, and the city saw serious unrest in the early 1830s. Over time, Jacquard weaving became standard for brocades, damasks, tapestries and furnishing fabrics in many countries.

The system of punched cards also influenced other fields. Charles Babbage proposed using similar cards to give instructions to his Analytical Engine, and later data-processing machines adopted punched cards for storing information. Modern electronic Jacquard looms use computer-controlled actuators rather than cards, but they preserve the principle of selecting individual warp threads according to a stored design.

title: Tapestry Weaving Traditions
text:
Tapestry Weaving Traditions

Tapestry is a form of weft-faced weaving in which the weft threads, usually in many colours, are worked back and forth across only the areas where each colour is needed. The warp threads are stretched on a loom and are almost entirely hidden by the weft, so that the finished cloth carries a pattern or picture as an integral part of its structure rather than as surface decoration. Because colours are built up in small sections, the technique lends itself to pictorial designs, geometric motifs and detailed ornament. Tapestry is found in many regions of the world and has been produced on simple frame looms as well as on large, specialised workshop looms.

Technique and Equipment

Tapestry weavers work on either vertical (high-warp) or horizontal (low-warp) looms. In both cases the warp is held under tension, and the weaver passes coloured wefts through it by hand, often with small bobbins or with the fingers alone. The weft is then packed down with a comb or beater so that it covers the warp completely. Where two areas of colour meet along a vertical line, the weaver must decide how to join them. Slits may be left open, giving a crisp edge that is often used deliberately; wefts may be interlocked with each other; or they may be wrapped around a shared warp. Each solution affects the strength, texture and appearance of the cloth. Hatching, in which wefts of different colours are interlaced in small wedges, is used to create gradual shading.

European Workshop Traditions

In medieval and Renaissance Europe, tapestry became closely associated with large urban workshops, particularly in the Low Countries and northern France. Towns such as Arras, Tournai, Brussels and Paris developed organised industries in which designers, painters and weavers each played a role. Artists prepared designs known as cartoons, which weavers followed closely, often working from the reverse side of the cloth. Wool was the principal material, frequently enriched with silk and with threads wrapped in precious metal. Large hangings depicting religious subjects, hunting scenes, history and allegory were used to decorate and insulate the halls of churches and palaces, and they could be transported from one residence to another. Royal and private manufactories, such as the Gobelins in France, continued the tradition in later centuries, and a revival of tapestry in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries involved artists and craft workers who sought to renew its status as an art form.

Andean Traditions

In the Andean region of South America, tapestry weaving has a very long history. Textiles made by cultures such as the Wari, Tiwanaku and Inca include tapestry-woven tunics and hangings of fine camelid wool and cotton, with dense, stylised designs. Cloth held exceptional social and ritual value, and in some periods its production was organised by the state. Weaving is still practised in highland communities, where patterned cloth continues to communicate regional and community identity.

Middle Eastern and Central Asian Traditions

Flat-woven tapestry techniques are central to the kilim of Anatolia, the Caucasus, Iran and neighbouring lands. Kilims are made mainly of wool, using the slit technique and bold geometric motifs whose meanings vary by region and family. Many were woven by women for domestic use as floor coverings, bags, cushions and wall hangings. Related slit-tapestry cloths are also made in Central Asia and in parts of the Balkans.

East Asian Traditions

In China, a tapestry technique known as kesi uses silk wefts that are woven in separate areas, leaving small slits between colour fields. Kesi was valued at court for robes, panels and reproductions of paintings and calligraphy. Similar silk tapestry methods were used in Japan, where the related tsuzure-ori technique appears in ceremonial textiles and obi.

Other Traditions

Tapestry weaving also developed in Scandinavia, where long-established techniques produced narrative hangings and coverlets, and among Indigenous peoples of North America. The Navajo, for example, weave wool textiles with tapestry techniques, and their designs have changed over time in response to new materials and markets. Together these traditions show how a shared structural principle has been adapted to suit local materials, purposes and aesthetics.

title: Ikat: Resist-Dyed Yarn Weaving
text:
Ikat: Resist-Dyed Yarn Weaving

Ikat is a method of patterning cloth in which the yarns are resist-dyed before weaving begins. The word comes from the Malay and Indonesian term mengikat, meaning "to tie" or "to bind," and it describes the central step of the process: sections of yarn are bound tightly so that dye cannot penetrate them. When the bound yarns are later set up on a loom and woven, the dyed and undyed areas combine to form designs. Because the pattern is created in the yarn rather than on the finished fabric, ikat is distinct from printing, painting, and embroidery, and it is related in principle to other resist techniques such as batik and tie-dye, which are applied to woven cloth.

Technique

The process begins with the preparation of the yarn, which may be cotton, silk, bast fibre, or wool. The yarn is stretched on a frame in bundles that correspond to the length and width of the intended cloth. Weavers then tie off the areas that are to remain the colour of the undyed fibre. Traditional binding materials include palm leaf strips, cotton thread, and raffia, and modern practitioners sometimes use rubber bands or plastic strips. The bundle is immersed in a dye bath, and the binding is removed or altered. Additional sections may then be bound or uncovered so that further colours can be added in successive baths. Complex designs in several colours may require a long series of tying and dyeing stages before any weaving can start.

Ikat is classified according to which yarns carry the resist pattern. In warp ikat, only the lengthwise threads are dyed in this way, and the design appears as the warp is aligned on the loom. In weft ikat, the crosswise threads carry the pattern, and the weaver must place each pick carefully to keep the design clear. Double ikat, in which both warp and weft are resist-dyed, is the most demanding form, since the two sets of threads must be matched exactly as the cloth is woven. A characteristic feature of all ikat is a soft, slightly blurred edge to the motifs, caused by small movements of the yarns during weaving and by dye seeping beneath the bindings. This feathered outline is generally regarded as a mark of the technique rather than a flaw.

Regional traditions

Ikat is found across a wide part of the world, and scholars continue to discuss whether it arose independently in several places or spread along trade routes. In Indonesia, the islands of Sumba, Flores, and Timor are known for warp ikat textiles that were historically tied to ceremonial exchange, status, and funerary customs. In Bali, the village of Tenganan Pegeringsingan preserves a double ikat cloth called geringsing, which is associated with ritual use.

In India, the patola of Gujarat is a double ikat silk sari with a long history of trade and prestige, while Odisha and Telangana produce ikat in cotton and silk, including the pochampally designs. Japan has a related tradition known as kasuri, often woven in indigo-dyed cotton. In Central Asia, the Uzbek ikat known as abr, meaning "cloud," was produced in silk and used for robes and hangings in Bukhara, Samarkand, and the Fergana Valley. Yemen, Guatemala, Mexico, Peru, and parts of West Africa also have ikat traditions. In Guatemala and Mexico, the technique is often used for the rebozo shawl and for skirt cloth, and is commonly called jaspe.

Cultural significance

In many communities, ikat textiles serve social and religious purposes. They may be worn at weddings, offered as gifts between families, wrapped around the dead, or kept as heirlooms. Motifs often refer to ancestors, animals, plants, or protective forces, and particular patterns have sometimes been reserved for nobility or ritual specialists. Natural dyes such as indigo, madder, and lac have long been used, although synthetic dyes are now widespread. Today ikat survives through both household production and workshops, and it has also been adopted by fashion and interior design, which has raised concerns about imitation and the fair support of traditional weavers.

title: Supplementary Weft and Songket Brocade
text:
Supplementary Weft and Songket Brocade

Supplementary weft techniques are methods of weaving in which an extra set of weft threads is added to a ground cloth to create pattern. The ground fabric is complete without these additional threads, which are inserted only where a motif is wanted and which float on the surface or are bound into the cloth at intervals. Because the pattern threads are separate from the structural threads, weavers can use materials that would be too costly or too fragile for the whole fabric, such as metallic thread, silk, or heavily dyed cotton. The resulting textiles are often described as brocaded, although the term is applied in several ways in the literature, and some authors reserve it for patterns made on a drawloom.

Basic Principles

In a typical supplementary weft cloth, the weaver passes a ground weft through the shed in the usual manner and then inserts a pattern weft across only part of the width of the warp. The pattern weft may be carried by a small shuttle, a bobbin, or a fine stick, and it is often picked up by hand with a pointed tool. Where the pattern thread is not needed, it is either cut off or left to pass across the back of the cloth. The choice between these approaches affects the appearance of the reverse side and the durability of the piece. Weavers working in this manner may follow a design held in memory, a pattern counted from an existing cloth, or a set of cords or lifted sticks that record the sequence of threads to be raised.

Songket

Songket is the best-known supplementary weft tradition of maritime Southeast Asia. It is woven in parts of Sumatra, the Malay Peninsula, Borneo, Bali, Lombok, Sulawesi, and neighbouring areas, and it is associated with courts, ceremonial dress, and marriage. The name is commonly connected to a Malay verb meaning to hook or to pick out, which describes the way in which the weaver lifts selected warp threads and inserts the gold or silver weft beneath them. Some scholars propose a different origin for the word, and its history remains a matter of discussion.

Songket is usually woven on a frame loom or a backstrap loom with a plain or twill ground in silk or cotton. The metallic pattern thread was traditionally made by wrapping a thin strip of precious metal around a core, while later cloths frequently use commercially produced gilt or synthetic metallic yarns. The pattern weft is inserted by hand, one motif at a time, so that a finished length may take many weeks or months to complete. The motifs are often drawn from plants, such as bamboo shoots, rice, and flowering vines, as well as from geometric forms. Many patterns carry names and meanings, and in some regions certain designs were restricted to royalty or to people of high rank.

Regional Variation

Palembang in southern Sumatra has long been regarded as a major centre, and its cloths are known for dense gold patterning over a richly coloured ground. The Minangkabau of western Sumatra produce songket that is closely tied to custom and is worn at weddings and other formal occasions. In Terengganu and Kelantan on the east coast of the Malay Peninsula, weavers have developed their own motif repertoires and colour preferences, and the cloth remains a marker of regional identity. In Bali, songket is used for temple dress and dance costume, and in Lombok it forms part of village ceremonial attire. Each of these traditions has its own proportions of ground and ornament, although the underlying technique is shared.

Related Traditions

Supplementary weft patterning appears widely beyond Southeast Asia. Examples include the brocaded silks of India, notably the cloths of Varanasi, the inlaid patterns of Scandinavian and Scottish weaving, the brocaded huipils of Guatemala and southern Mexico, and the decorated cotton cloths of West Africa. In each case, the extra weft allows a decorative surface to be built on a simple structural cloth. Today many such crafts are maintained by cooperatives and heritage programmes, and the transmission of skill from older weavers to younger ones is a continuing concern.

title: Kente and West African Strip Weaving
text:
Kente and West African Strip Weaving

Strip weaving is one of the most widespread and distinctive cloth-making traditions of West Africa. Rather than producing a single broad web of fabric, weavers make long, narrow bands on a loom, then cut them into lengths and sew them edge to edge to form a larger cloth. The method is found across the savanna and forest regions, from the Sahel to the Gulf of Guinea, and its best-known product is kente, the woven cloth of the Asante and Ewe peoples of Ghana and neighbouring Togo.

The Loom and the Technique

Strip weavers traditionally use a horizontal loom fitted with heddles worked by foot pedals. The warp is stretched over a long distance and weighted at one end, and the weaver advances it gradually as the cloth grows. Because the loom is narrow, the work is steady and repetitive, and a finished strip may be very long before it is cut. In much of West Africa, including Asante and Ewe communities, this work has been done mainly by men, often within families or guilds that pass skills from one generation to the next. Among the Yoruba of Nigeria, both men on narrow looms and women on broader upright looms have produced distinct kinds of cloth.

Kente

The word kente is usually linked to a term in the Twi language meaning basket, a reference to the woven appearance of the cloth. Asante tradition places the origin of kente in the town of Bonwire, where two weavers are said to have learned their craft by watching a spider build its web. Whatever its historical origin, kente developed under royal patronage, and for a long period certain designs were reserved for the Asante king and members of the court. Ewe weavers, working in towns such as Agotime and Kpetoe, developed their own styles, which often include pictorial motifs and a greater variety of inlaid figures.

Much of kente's visual character comes from the way supplementary weft threads create blocks of pattern across a plain ground. Strips are then arranged so that the patterns of neighbouring bands offset or complement one another. Early weavers are recorded as unravelling imported silk cloth and reweaving the thread into their own designs, alongside locally spun cotton. Later, rayon and other commercially produced yarns became common, widening the range of colour available.

Pattern, Colour and Meaning

Individual kente designs carry names, and these names often refer to proverbs, historical events, people, or moral qualities. One well-known Asante design is called adweneasa, a term often translated as "my skill is exhausted," which is said to commemorate a weaver's most elaborate composition. Colours are also read symbolically, though interpretations vary by region, period and wearer. Gold is commonly associated with status and wealth, green with growth and renewal, blue with peace and affection, red with spiritual intensity or sacrifice, and black with maturity and spiritual strength. These associations are best understood as customary guides rather than fixed rules.

Use and Social Role

Kente is worn draped over the body, typically as a large wrapper, on occasions such as festivals, weddings, funerals, naming ceremonies and state events. The choice of cloth signals rank, occasion and the wearer's relationship to the community. In the twentieth century, kente also acquired wider significance as a symbol of Ghanaian national identity after independence in 1957, and later as a sign of African heritage among communities in the diaspora. Stoles of kente are now frequently worn at graduation ceremonies.

Other Strip-Weaving Traditions

Kente belongs to a larger family of West African strip-woven textiles. The Yoruba produce aso oke, a prestige cloth worn at ceremonies and often made in sets of wrapper, head tie and shoulder cloth. The Igbo town of Akwete is known for a broad, richly patterned cloth woven by women. In the Sahel, Fulani weavers make wool blankets with bold bands of colour, and Hausa and Mande weavers produce cotton strips that may be dyed or later decorated, as in the mud-dyed bogolan cloth of Mali.

Contemporary Issues

Printed and machine-made imitations of kente patterns are now widely sold, which has raised concerns about the livelihoods of hand weavers and about the protection of traditional designs. Ghana has taken steps to register and promote authentic cloth, and weaving centres continue to train new weavers and to supply both ceremonial and export markets.

title: Navajo (Diné) Weaving
text:
Navajo (Diné) Weaving

Navajo weaving is the textile tradition of the Diné, the Navajo people of the American Southwest, whose homeland lies in present-day Arizona, New Mexico, and Utah. Woven on upright looms, Navajo textiles are known for their dense structure, geometric design, and a long history of adaptation to changing materials and markets. Weaving has traditionally been practiced mainly by women, though men also weave today, and the craft remains an important source of income, artistic expression, and cultural continuity.

Origins and Traditional Accounts

Diné oral tradition holds that weaving was taught by Spider Woman (Na'ashjéii Asdzáá), a holy being who instructed the people in the use of the loom, and by Spider Man, who is said to have shown how its frame should be built. In these accounts, the loom's parts are linked to the natural world: the upright posts and crossbeams are associated with the sky, the earth, and the sun's light. Many weavers continue to observe teachings about respect for the craft, and some include a deliberate feature in the border of a rug, often called a spirit line or weaver's pathway, whose meaning varies among families and communities.

Historians generally agree that the Navajo learned some weaving techniques from Pueblo neighbors, probably during the seventeenth century, and that Spanish colonization introduced Churro sheep, whose long, straight, low-grease wool proved well suited to hand spinning and weaving. Cotton had earlier been woven by Pueblo peoples, but wool became the principal Navajo fiber.

Loom and Technique

The Navajo loom is a vertical frame, traditionally made of wooden poles and set up either outdoors or in a dwelling. The warp is wound continuously around top and bottom beams, so the finished textile has four finished selvage edges and no cut warp ends. The weaver works while seated, building the pattern from the bottom upward. Shed rods and heddles separate the warp threads, and a wooden batten and weaving comb are used to pack the weft tightly.

The primary structure is tapestry weave, in which the weft completely covers the warp. Diagonal lines, sometimes called lazy lines, are created when a weaver works a section of the textile in an arc rather than across the full width. Twill and a related technique called twill weave appear in some regional styles, and the two-faced weave produces different patterns on each side.

Wool Preparation and Dyes

Preparing the wool is a labor-intensive process. Fleece is cleaned, carded, and spun on a hand spindle, often in several passes to make the yarn finer and stronger. Traditional dyes derive from plants, minerals, and insects. Rabbitbrush, juniper, sumac, and various roots yield yellows, golds, browns, and greens, while indigo, obtained through trade, produced blues. Natural wool shades of white, gray, brown, and black are also used without dyeing. From the nineteenth century, commercial yarns and aniline dyes became widely available, and many weavers adopted them; others have continued or revived the use of vegetal dyes.

Historical Development

Early Diné textiles included wearing blankets, dresses, and sashes. Chief blankets, with broad horizontal stripes, were widely traded among Indigenous nations of the Plains and Southwest. After the forced removal and internment known as the Long Walk and the confinement at Bosque Redondo in the 1860s, the Navajo returned to their homeland and the weaving economy changed. The expansion of railways and trading posts in the later nineteenth century brought new yarns and new customers. Traders encouraged weavers to make heavier, rug-like textiles for sale to non-Native buyers, and the blanket gradually gave way to the rug as the typical product.

Regional Styles

Distinct styles developed in different parts of the Navajo Nation, often named for trading posts or communities. Common examples include:

Ganado, noted for deep red grounds with black, white, and gray patterns.
Two Grey Hills, characterized by fine weaving in natural undyed wool tones.
Teec Nos Pos, known for elaborate designs with bold outlines and bright colors.
Crystal, which often features banded designs in soft vegetal-dyed colors.
Storm Pattern, a design with a central rectangle linked by zigzag lines to corners.
Pictorial rugs, which depict figures, landscapes, or scenes of daily life.

Contemporary Practice

Today Navajo weavers work within and beyond these traditions, and their textiles are sold through markets, galleries, and auctions. Organizations on the reservation and elsewhere support apprenticeships, wool production, and fair pricing. Concerns about imitation goods led to federal legislation protecting the authenticity of Native American-made crafts. Younger weavers continue to explore new color palettes and designs while drawing on the teachings of earlier generations.

title: Andean Textile Traditions
text:
Andean Textile Traditions

Textile production in the Andean region of South America is among the oldest and most continuous craft traditions in the world. Cloth has long carried social, economic, and ceremonial meaning in the highland and coastal societies of present-day Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador, and neighbouring areas. Before the Spanish conquest in the sixteenth century, woven goods were valued as highly as, and in some contexts more highly than, metal. They served as clothing, as offerings, as markers of rank, and as items of tribute and exchange.

Early Developments

Archaeological evidence shows that fibre technologies were well established on the Peruvian coast thousands of years before the Inca state. Early cultures worked cotton and, in the highlands, the fibres of camelids. Twining, looping, and weaving techniques appear in the early record, and the dry coastal climate has preserved fabrics from cultures such as Paracas, Nazca, Wari, and Chimú. Paracas funerary bundles from the southern coast contain richly embroidered mantles with figures rendered in many colours. Later Wari tunics show tapestry weaving of great technical precision. Under the Inca, a specialised class of cloth makers, including the *acllakuna* (chosen women) and male weavers known as *cumbicamayoc*, produced fine cloth called *cumbi* for the state and for religious use.

Fibres

Andean weavers draw on a distinctive range of materials. Cotton, grown in coastal valleys, was one of the earliest. In the highlands, the main fibres come from four camelid species: the domesticated llama and alpaca, and the wild vicuña and guanaco. Alpaca fleece is valued for its softness and range of natural shades. Vicuña fibre, extremely fine, was historically reserved for elites. Sheep's wool was introduced by the Spanish and is now widely used alongside native fibres.

Spinning and Weaving

Spinning is traditionally done by hand with a drop spindle, and it is often carried out while walking or tending animals. Two principal loom types are used. The backstrap loom, in which the weaver's body tension holds the warp taut, is common among women and is suited to narrow, intricately patterned bands and cloths. The horizontal staked-out ground loom and, after the colonial period, the European treadle loom are also used, the latter chiefly by men for wider cloth.

Structure and pattern are central to Andean weaving. Warp-faced techniques, in which the vertical threads dominate the surface, allow complex supplementary-warp designs, often called pallay in Quechua. Tapestry, double cloth, and discontinuous warp and weft were all developed to high levels in the pre-Columbian period. Many designs are geometric or stylised representations of animals, plants, and landscape features, and patterns often identify the community of the weaver.

Dyeing

Andean dyers have long used plant, insect, and mineral sources. Cochineal, an insect that lives on prickly pear cactus, yields crimson and red shades and became an important export after the conquest. Indigo and related plants provide blues, while various local plants, lichens, and barks give yellows, greens, and browns. Mordants, including minerals and fermented plant materials, help fix colour. Natural dyeing continues in many communities, sometimes alongside synthetic dyes introduced in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

Cultural Role and Continuity

Textiles remain integral to identity and ritual in Quechua and Aymara communities. Garments such as the woman's shawl (*lliclla*), the carrying cloth (*manta* or *q'ipi*), woven belts, and ponchos communicate community and status. Woven bundles are used in festivals and offerings.

In the late twentieth century, weaving cooperatives and cultural centres, such as those in the Cusco region of Peru, began to document older techniques and support weavers' livelihoods. These efforts aim to preserve knowledge passed down through families, while enabling weavers to sell their work in wider markets on their own terms.

title: Carpet and Rug Weaving
text:
Carpet and Rug Weaving

Carpet and rug weaving is among the oldest and most widely practised textile crafts, producing floor coverings, wall hangings, saddle bags, tent furnishings and prayer mats. Although the two terms overlap, "carpet" usually refers to a larger floor covering and "rug" to a smaller one. Techniques fall into two broad groups: pile weaving, in which short lengths of yarn are knotted or looped into a foundation, and flat weaving, in which the design is formed by interlacing warp and weft alone.

Materials and Preparation

Wool is the most common fibre, valued for its resilience, its ability to hold dye and its natural insulation. Weavers also use silk, cotton, goat hair, camel hair and, in some regions, jute or other plant fibres. Cotton is frequently used for the warp and weft of the foundation, while wool or silk forms the pile. Preparation traditionally includes shearing, washing, carding, spinning and dyeing. Many weaving communities dye their yarns with plant, insect and mineral sources, such as madder root for reds, indigo for blues and various leaves, bark and hulls for yellows, browns and greens. Synthetic dyes were introduced in the nineteenth century and are now common, though natural dyeing has been revived by many workshops.

Looms

Looms may be horizontal or vertical. Nomadic and village weavers often use a horizontal ground loom, which can be staked out on the ground and dismantled when a household moves. Workshop weavers more commonly use a vertical loom, on which the warp threads are stretched between two beams and the weaver works from the bottom upward. Some vertical looms have a roller mechanism that allows the finished portion to be wound away, making longer carpets possible. Weavers beat down each row of wefts with a comb or a heavy fork-like tool to produce a firm, even structure.

Pile Weaving and Knots

In knotted-pile rugs, short lengths of yarn are tied around pairs of warp threads in rows, and the ends are cut to form the surface. Two knots are widely recognised. The symmetrical knot, often called the Turkish or Ghiordes knot, encircles two warp threads and is common in Anatolia, the Caucasus and parts of Central Asia. The asymmetrical knot, often called the Persian or Senneh knot, is wrapped around one warp thread and passes beside the next, and is associated with Iran, India and Pakistan, as well as parts of China. The fineness of a rug depends largely on knot size and density, and the finest examples, often woven in silk, display intricate curvilinear designs.

After weaving, the pile is trimmed, and the rug is washed and stretched. Designs may be memorised, passed down within families, or followed from a drawn pattern called a cartoon, which in some workshops is read aloud by a master to the weavers.

Flat Weaves

Flat-woven rugs include kilims, soumak, dhurries and similar types. The kilim, made across Anatolia, the Balkans, the Caucasus and Central Asia, is formed by weaving coloured wefts back and forth within their own pattern areas, often leaving small slits where colours meet. Soumak is a weft-wrapping technique that produces a sturdier surface resembling embroidery. Dhurries, from South Asia, are traditionally cotton flat weaves used as bedding and floor covers.

Regional Traditions

Persian carpets are known for medallion layouts, garden designs and floral motifs, with notable centres historically including Tabriz, Isfahan, Kashan and Kerman. Anatolian rugs often feature bold geometric forms and prayer-niche designs. Caucasian weaving favours stylised animals and angular medallions, while Turkmen weavers produce carpets with repeated guls, or emblematic motifs, in deep reds. In Morocco, Berber women weave pile and flat rugs with abstract symbols that vary by tribe and region, and in Scandinavia the rya and rölakan traditions developed their own shaggy and tapestry-like forms. Tibetan rugs, traditionally used as seat covers and sleeping mats, are woven with a distinctive looped technique. Navajo weavers of the American Southwest developed a flat-woven rug tradition after the arrival of Spanish sheep, and it became a significant craft economy in the late nineteenth century.

Cultural Significance

Rugs have long served as dowry items, gifts, devotional objects and trade goods. Motifs may carry protective, religious or tribal meanings, though interpretations are often debated by scholars. Today the craft faces pressure from machine production and shifting labour patterns, while cooperatives, museums and fair-trade initiatives work to sustain skills and support weavers.

title: Band Weaving and Tablet Weaving
text:
Band Weaving and Tablet Weaving

Band weaving is the production of narrow woven strips, generally used as belts, straps, garters, trims, headbands, ties and bindings. Because the finished piece is narrow, it can be made with simple, portable equipment, and the technique has developed independently in many regions. Bands are often valued for strength as well as decoration, and in many communities they have carried social meaning, marking age, marital status, kinship or office.

Principal methods

Several approaches are used to make bands. In the first, a narrow warp is stretched on a small loom, such as a rigid-heddle loom, and woven in the usual way with a weft passing through alternating sets of threads. In the second, the weaver uses a backstrap arrangement, tying one end of the warp to a fixed point, such as a post or tree, and the other to a belt around the waist. Body tension is adjusted by leaning forward or back. The third method is tablet weaving, described below. A fourth group of techniques, including finger-loop braiding and sprang, produces band-like structures without a conventional loom, though these are sometimes classed separately from true weaving.

Rigid-heddle and inkle weaving

The rigid heddle is a flat frame with slots and holes through which warp threads pass. Raising or lowering it creates the shed, or opening, for the weft. Bands of this kind are made across Europe, Asia and the Americas. The inkle loom, a small frame loom with pegs that hold the warp, became popular in northern Europe and later in North America. It is well suited to warp-faced bands, in which the closely spaced warp threads completely cover the weft and form the pattern.

Backstrap band weaving

In the Andes, weavers in many highland communities make bands with intricate warp-faced patterns, often using supplementary warp techniques in which extra threads float on the surface to create figures such as animals, plants and geometric motifs. In Southeast Asia and parts of Central America, backstrap weavers also produce narrow patterned cloths and belts. Patterns are frequently learned by observation and memorised, although some weavers keep sample strips as references.

Tablet weaving

Tablet weaving, also called card weaving, uses a set of small flat tablets, traditionally made from wood, bone, horn or leather, and today often from cardboard or plastic. Each tablet has holes at its corners, and a warp thread passes through each hole. The tablets are stacked and the weft is inserted through the opening formed between the upper and lower threads. When the tablets are turned together, the threads change position and the shed is renewed. By turning some tablets forward and others backward, or by changing the colour order in the threading, the weaver creates diagonal lines, diamonds, chevrons and other designs.

The resulting bands are strong, firm and slightly twisted in structure, which makes them suitable for belts, straps and edgings. Tablet weaving can also be combined with brocading, in which an additional weft of a contrasting thread is laid in to form figures.

Historical evidence

The origin of tablet weaving is debated. Archaeological finds of tablets and bands have been reported from sites in Europe, the Near East and Asia. Bands woven by this method have been recovered from Iron Age burials in northern Europe, and from early medieval graves in Anglo-Saxon and Scandinavian contexts. Medieval European sources show tablet-woven braids used on vestments, as borders on garments, and on book bindings. In Egypt, a well-known band associated with the reign of Ramesses II is often cited in discussions of early tablet weaving, though its interpretation has been discussed by scholars.

Survival and contemporary practice

Tablet weaving continued as a living tradition in parts of the Balkans, the Caucasus, North Africa, the Middle East and Central and South Asia, where bands are made for belts, animal trappings and tent fittings. In recent decades, historical re-enactors, craft guilds and hand-weavers have revived the technique, and researchers have reconstructed ancient patterns from archaeological fragments. Band weaving remains a practical craft, requiring few tools and little space, and it continues to serve both everyday and ceremonial uses.

title: Plant-Based Natural Dye Sources
text:
Plant-Based Natural Dye Sources

Plants have supplied colour to textiles for as long as people have spun and woven fibre. Roots, leaves, flowers, bark, seeds, fruits, and wood all contain pigments or pigment precursors that can be extracted in water and fixed to cloth or yarn. Across Asia, Africa, the Americas, and Europe, communities developed dye traditions around the plants that grew locally or could be obtained through trade. The resulting palettes reflect regional ecology as much as cultural preference.

Blue: Indigo-Bearing Plants

Indigo is among the most widely used and historically significant dyestuffs. The blue pigment is not present in the living leaf in a usable form. Instead, the leaves of several species contain colourless compounds that must be released and chemically transformed. Indigofera tinctoria was cultivated extensively in South Asia and became a major trade commodity. In temperate Europe, woad (Isatis tinctoria) served a similar purpose and was grown for centuries before imported indigo displaced it. In East Asia, Persicaria tinctoria, often called Japanese indigo, underlies the aizome tradition, while in West Africa, species of Lonchocarpus and Indigofera have long been used by Yoruba and other dyers to produce deep blue cloth.

Indigo is applied through a vat process. The pigment is made soluble by reduction, often through fermentation, and the cloth is dipped in the yellowish-green liquid. Exposure to air then oxidises the pigment, turning the fabric blue. Repeated dipping produces progressively darker shades.

Red: Roots, Insects, and Woods

Madder (Rubia tinctorum) has been used in Europe, the Middle East, and Central Asia, and related species such as Rubia cordifolia, known as manjistha or Indian madder, were important in South Asia. The red colour comes from anthraquinone compounds in the roots, which require a mordant to bind well to fibre. Different mordants shift the colour toward orange, rose, or deep red.

Other red sources include sappanwood (Biancaea sappan) and brazilwood, which yield reddish to purplish tones, and safflower (Carthamus tinctorius), whose petals give both yellow and a more delicate red. Although cochineal and lac are produced by insects rather than plants, they were often used alongside plant dyes and, in the case of cochineal, feed on cactus.

Yellow and Orange

Yellow dyes are found in a great variety of plants. Weld (Reseda luteola) was a principal European source and is valued for its relatively clear, bright tone. Turmeric (Curcuma longa) gives a vivid yellow widely used in South and Southeast Asia, though it fades readily in light. Pomegranate rind, onion skins, marigold flowers, and the bark of various trees provide additional yellows, golds, and browns. Annatto seeds from Bixa orellana yield orange and were used in Central and South America.

Brown, Black, and Grey

Tannin-rich materials are central to dyeing in these tones. Oak galls, walnut hulls, alder bark, myrobalan fruit, and catechu from Acacia species all contain tannins that produce tan, brown, or dark shades. When combined with iron salts, tannins can yield grey or black. Mud dyeing, practised in parts of West Africa and in Japan's Amami Islands, pairs tannin-bearing plant extracts with iron-rich mud to create deep, lasting black.

Green and Purple

True green plant dyes are uncommon, so green is usually achieved by overdyeing blue with yellow. Purples are obtained from sources such as logwood (Haematoxylum campechianum), lichens used to make orchil, and certain berries, though many of these are less lightfast.

Mordants and Fastness

Many plant dyes depend on mordants, typically metal salts such as alum, to fix colour to fibre. Traditional dyers also used plant-based mordants, including ash lye and tannin-rich materials. Colourfastness varies with the dye, fibre, and mordant, and has long influenced which plants were prized and which were treated as minor or temporary colourants.

title: Insect and Mollusc Dyes: Cochineal, Kermes, and Tyrian Purple
text:
Insect and Mollusc Dyes: Cochineal, Kermes, and Tyrian Purple

Among the many natural colourants used in traditional textile crafts, a small group derived from animals has held a special place. Red dyes obtained from scale insects and purple dyes obtained from sea snails were costly to produce, difficult to standardise, and prized for their brilliance and durability. Because of this, they became associated with rank, ceremony, and long-distance trade in many societies.

Kermes

Kermes is a red dye made from the dried bodies of female scale insects of the genus Kermes, which live on certain oak trees around the Mediterranean basin. The insects were collected by hand, and the material that was sold looked like small berry-like grains. The Greek and Latin names for the dye gave rise to the English word "crimson", and the use of the term "in grain" for a deep, fast colour is also linked to these grains.

Kermes was used in the ancient Mediterranean and western Asia and remained a principal source of scarlet in medieval Europe. Woollen cloth dyed with it was a mark of wealth in the cloth-producing towns of Italy, Flanders, and England. The dye is usually applied with an aluminium-based mordant, and the resulting shades range from orange-red to a deep, slightly bluish crimson, depending on the mordant, the water, and any additional dyes. The colour is fairly resistant to light and washing.

Cochineal

Cochineal comes from a different insect, Dactylopius coccus, which feeds on prickly pear cacti and is native to the Americas. Its colouring matter, carminic acid, is present in higher concentration than the equivalent compound in kermes, so less material was needed to produce a strong colour. Peoples of Mesoamerica and the Andes cultivated the insect long before European contact. It was used in textiles such as the woven and embroidered cloths of Oaxaca, and in the camelid-fibre textiles of the Andes.

After the Spanish conquest of the sixteenth century, cochineal became one of the major exports of the colonial economy. Shipments crossed the Atlantic and were distributed across Europe and to Asia. It gradually replaced kermes, because it gave a stronger and more brilliant colour. It was used for the scarlet cloth of military uniforms, for the robes of church and state officials, and for carpets and tapestries. Spanish authorities guarded information about the source of the dye, and for some time Europeans disagreed about whether it was an animal or a seed.

Cochineal colours vary with treatment. With an aluminium mordant it yields crimson and scarlet; with tin, a brighter red; with iron, greys and purples. Acidity or alkalinity in the dye bath moves the shade toward orange or violet. Cultivation continued in parts of Mexico, Peru, and the Canary Islands, and the dye is still used by hand weavers and in some commercial products.

Tyrian Purple

Tyrian purple, also called shellfish purple, was obtained from the secretions of several species of predatory sea snails of the family Muricidae, including Murex brandaris, Hexaplex trunculus, and Stramonita haemastoma. The glands of the animals were extracted, and the secretion was exposed to air and light, during which it turned through yellow and green to purple. Unlike most dyes, it required no separate mordant.

The dye is associated with Phoenician cities such as Tyre and Sidon, and heaps of crushed shells have been found at ancient dyeing sites around the Mediterranean. In the Roman and Byzantine worlds, purple cloth was regulated by law or custom and became a sign of imperial and senatorial office. The knowledge of the process declined in Europe following the fall of Constantinople in 1453, as other dyes and sources of red and purple filled the same social role.

Legacy

These dyes illustrate how a raw material can shape trade, law, and craft practice. The labour involved in gathering tiny insects or large numbers of snails explains their high price. Synthetic dyes introduced in the nineteenth century displaced them from most commercial use, but they continue in heritage textile work, conservation research, and the practice of artisans who value their historical associations.

title: Mordants and Color Fixation
text:
Mordants and Color Fixation

Many natural dyestuffs will stain a fiber but will not remain in it. Without a means of binding the coloring matter to the material, the color tends to fade in sunlight or wash out in water. In traditional textile practice, the substances and techniques used to prevent this are known as mordants, a term derived from the Latin mordere, "to bite." Although the old idea that a mordant literally bites into the fiber is not accurate, the term has persisted. Modern descriptions explain the effect in terms of chemistry: a mordant, usually a metal salt, forms a coordination complex with both the dye molecule and the functional groups of the fiber, creating an insoluble link between them.

Substantive and Adjective Dyes

Dyes are often divided into two broad groups according to how they behave. Substantive dyes attach to fiber directly, with no preparatory treatment. Some tannin-rich plant materials and a few lichen dyes are used in this way. Adjective dyes, which include madder, weld, cochineal, and many others, need a mordant to produce strong and lasting color. Indigo belongs to neither group in the usual sense. It is a vat dye, which is made soluble by chemical reduction, absorbed by the fiber, and then returned to its insoluble blue form by exposure to air. Because of this, indigo has historically been fixed without a metallic mordant.

Common Mordants

Alum, a potassium aluminium sulfate, has been the most widely used mordant across many cultures. It is valued because it gives bright, clear colors and has little effect on the hue of the dye. Alum mordanting is described in sources from the ancient Mediterranean, and the mineral was a major item of trade in the medieval and early modern periods. Iron, often applied as ferrous sulfate or as a liquor made by steeping rusted metal in vinegar or fermented liquid, tends to darken and dull colors, producing deep browns, grays, and blacks. Copper salts can shift colors toward green. Tin was adopted in Europe to brighten reds and oranges, notably with cochineal, though it can leave wool harsh and brittle if overused. Chromium compounds were introduced in the nineteenth century but are now discouraged because of toxicity.

The same dye can yield quite different colors depending on the mordant. Madder, for example, may give red with alum, a more brownish or purplish shade with iron, and an orange-leaning tone with other treatments. Dyers have long exploited this by dyeing several lengths of cloth in a single bath after applying different mordants to each.

Plant-Based and Local Mordants

In many regions, mordants came from local plants rather than mined minerals. Certain plants accumulate aluminium in their tissues, and ash or leaves from these species have been used as a mordant source. Examples include clubmoss in northern Europe and the leaves of Symplocos species in Indonesia, where they are used in batik and ikat dyeing. Tannins from oak galls, pomegranate rind, sumac, and myrobalan are used to prepare cellulose fibers such as cotton and linen, which hold mordants less readily than wool or silk. A common sequence is to treat the cotton with tannin first and then with an aluminium salt. In parts of South Asia, this approach underlies the production of mordant-dyed and resist-printed cottons, in which different mordants are applied to the cloth in patterns before it is dyed in madder or a related dyestuff.

Other Fixation Methods

Not all fixation depends on metals. Fermented urine, soured bran, and other biological preparations have been used in the preparation of dye baths and fibers. In some Japanese and West African traditions, soybean liquid or similar proteinaceous coatings are applied to cloth to improve color uptake. Heat, time, and the pH of the bath also strongly influence how well a color is retained.

Contemporary Concerns

Present-day natural dyers pay particular attention to the safety and environmental effects of mordants. Alum and iron are generally regarded as low in hazard when handled properly, while tin, copper, and chromium require more careful disposal of waste liquid. Because of this, many craftspeople favor aluminium, iron, and plant tannins.

title: Indigo Cultivation and Vat Dyeing
text:
Indigo Cultivation and Vat Dyeing

Indigo is among the oldest and most widely traded natural dyes. The blue pigment, chemically known as indigotin, is obtained from several unrelated plant species, and its use has been documented across Asia, Africa, the Americas and Europe. Because the pigment does not dissolve in water in its natural form, indigo dyeing relies on a distinctive chemical process that has been developed independently by many cultures and remains central to a number of living textile traditions.

Source Plants

The principal indigo-yielding plants differ by region. Species of the genus Indigofera, a group of leguminous shrubs, are the main source in South Asia, parts of Africa, and Central and South America. Indigofera tinctoria was cultivated in the Indian subcontinent for millennia and became one of the best-known trade commodities of the ancient and early modern world. In East Asia, including Japan, China and Korea, the dye is more often derived from Persicaria tinctoria, commonly called dyer's knotweed. In Europe, woad (Isatis tinctoria), a member of the cabbage family, served as the traditional blue dye until Indigofera indigo imported by sea began to displace it in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. In parts of West Africa, the vine Lonchocarpus cyanescens has long been used, and other regions rely on additional local species.

Cultivation and Harvest

Indigo plants generally prefer warm climates and well-drained soil, although woad and dyer's knotweed tolerate cooler conditions. Farmers typically sow seed in the growing season and harvest the leaves before or around flowering, when the precursor compounds in the foliage are most abundant. In some regions more than one cutting can be taken from the same plants in a season. Harvested leaves must be processed quickly, since the precursors begin to degrade soon after cutting.

Extracting the Pigment

Two broad approaches to extraction are found. In the first, fresh leaves are steeped in water and allowed to ferment. The liquid is then drained, aerated by beating or stirring, and the resulting blue sediment is collected, pressed and dried into cakes or powder. This method was used for much of the commercial indigo of South Asia and the colonial plantations of the Americas. In the second, leaves are composted rather than steeped. In Japan, the leaves of dyer's knotweed are piled, wetted and turned over a period of months to produce a fermented material called sukumo, which serves as the basis of the dye bath. European woad makers similarly formed harvested leaves into balls, which were later fermented into a dye-ready couch.

The Chemistry of the Vat

Indigotin is insoluble, so it cannot simply be dissolved and applied to cloth. It must first be chemically reduced to a soluble, pale yellow-green form known as leuco-indigo. Fibers are immersed in this solution and then lifted into the air, where oxygen converts the pigment back to its insoluble blue form, fixed within and on the fiber. Repeated dipping and airing deepen the shade, and dyers often describe a gradual progression from pale sky tones to near black-blue.

Traditional Vat Types

Reduction was historically achieved without synthetic chemicals. Fermentation vats use microorganisms, supplied by sources such as bran, fruit, dates, or madder, to consume oxygen and generate reducing conditions. An alkaline medium is maintained with wood ash lye, lime, or in some traditions stale urine. Japanese dyers maintain fermentation vats of sukumo with ash lye, wheat bran and sake, and skilled practitioners monitor a vat's health by its smell, color and the foam, sometimes called the flower, that forms on the surface. Other traditions, including those of West Africa, use long-lived vats that are fed and tended over years.

Resist Techniques

Indigo is frequently combined with resist methods, in which sections of cloth are protected from the dye. Examples include Japanese shibori and katazome, Indonesian and West African batik, and Yoruba adire, in which cassava paste or wax is applied before dyeing. Such techniques exploit the dye's tendency to remain on the surface of the cloth and produce sharply defined patterns.

Modern Context

Synthetic indigo, first commercialized in the late nineteenth century, replaced most natural production and is now used for denim and other industrial textiles. Natural indigo survives chiefly in artisan communities, where its cultivation, fermentation and vat management continue as skilled and culturally significant practices.

title: Batik and Wax-Resist Dyeing
text:
Batik and Wax-Resist Dyeing

Wax-resist dyeing is a method of patterning cloth in which molten wax is applied to selected areas of the fabric before it is dyed. The wax penetrates the fibres and prevents dye from reaching the covered areas. When the wax is later removed, the original colour of the cloth appears as a pattern against the dyed ground. The technique is most closely associated with the Indonesian island of Java, where it is known as batik, a word usually connected to Javanese terms for writing or dotting. Similar resist methods, using wax or other substances, have developed independently or through trade in many regions of Asia and Africa.

Process

Cloth, traditionally cotton or silk, is first washed to remove dressings and then often treated to help it accept dye. The design is sketched lightly, commonly in pencil, and wax is applied over the lines and areas that are to remain undyed. The cloth is then immersed in a dye bath. Because each dye colour is added over the one before it, dyers generally work from lighter shades to darker ones, applying and removing wax between stages. Wax is removed by scraping, or by immersing the cloth in hot water, and the cycle is repeated for each additional colour. A complex textile may require weeks or months of work.

The wax is usually a blend. Beeswax adheres firmly and resists penetration, while paraffin is more brittle. Resins and other additives adjust its flexibility and melting behaviour. When the wax cracks as the cloth is handled, dye seeps into the fissures and produces the fine, irregular veining that is considered characteristic of many batik cloths.

Tools

In Java, fine lines and dots are drawn with the canting, a small copper reservoir with a narrow spout attached to a handle. The maker fills it with hot wax and draws on the cloth much as with a pen. Spouts of different sizes produce different line widths. Broader areas may be covered with brushes. In the middle of the nineteenth century, the cap, a copper stamp dipped in wax, was introduced. It allowed repeating motifs to be produced far more quickly, and it made batik available to a wider market. Cloth made with the canting is often called batik tulis, or written batik, and is generally valued more highly than stamped work.

Dyes and colours

Traditional Javanese batik relies on natural dyes. Indigo produces blues, and brown tones come from soga, prepared from the bark of several trees. Red shades have been obtained from the roots of the mengkudu plant. The resulting palette of deep blue, brown and cream is strongly associated with the batik of the central Javanese court cities of Yogyakarta and Surakarta. Coastal centres on the north of the island, which had long contact with Chinese, Indian, Arab and European traders, developed brighter colours and motifs drawn from many sources. Synthetic dyes came into use from the late nineteenth century.

Motifs and meaning

Batik designs often carry social or symbolic meaning. Geometric patterns such as parang, a diagonal arrangement of stylised forms, and kawung, a repeating pattern of intersecting circles, were once restricted at the courts to members of the ruling households. Other patterns are worn at weddings, births or periods of mourning. In 2009, UNESCO inscribed Indonesian batik on its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, citing its role in marking stages of life and in transmitting cultural identity.

Other traditions

Wax resist is practised well beyond Java. Malaysia has its own batik traditions, notably in the east coast states, where designs are often painted freehand with brushes and favour large floral motifs. In southwestern China, the Miao, Bouyei and other peoples apply beeswax to hemp or cotton and dye it with indigo, using motifs that include spirals, birds and plants. In West Africa, factory-printed cloths known as wax prints were developed in the nineteenth century in imitation of Javanese batik, and they became deeply embedded in local dress and commerce. Among the Yoruba of Nigeria, the adire tradition produces indigo cloth by resist methods, in which cassava paste often serves in place of wax. Japan has related paste-resist techniques, such as katazome and tsutsugaki.

Today, batik is produced by village workshops, individual artists and large factories. Craft organisations and cultural institutions continue to support training in hand-drawn methods.
