title: Shibori and Japanese Resist Techniques
text:
Shibori and Japanese Resist Techniques

Shibori is the Japanese term for a family of methods in which cloth is shaped, bound, folded, stitched, or compressed before dyeing, so that the dye cannot reach certain areas evenly. The word derives from the verb shiboru, meaning to wring, squeeze, or press, and it describes the physical act of manipulating the fabric as much as the patterns that result. Unlike printing or painting, shibori relies on the cloth itself to create the design. The finished patterns tend to have soft, slightly blurred edges, and no two pieces are exactly alike.

Origins and History

Resist-dyed textiles have been found in many parts of Asia, and fragments of tied and stitched cloth survive from the Nara period, when objects were preserved in temple and court collections. By the Heian period, tie-dyed fabrics were known at the imperial court. In later centuries, shibori became widely used for garments, especially during the Edo period, when sumptuary laws limited the display of costly silks and brocades among the merchant classes. Elaborate dyeing and stitching offered an alternative form of refinement that was less easily regulated.

Regional centers developed their own specialties. Arimatsu and Narumi, towns on the old Tōkaidō road near present-day Nagoya, became famous for cotton shibori sold to travelers. Kyoto was associated with fine silk work, including kanoko shibori, a dense pattern of tiny tied dots that resembles the spots on a fawn. Because every dot is bound by hand, kanoko work is among the most labor-intensive of all textile decoration.

Principal Techniques

Several broad categories are generally recognized.

Kumo shibori involves pleating or gathering fabric and binding it with thread, producing radiating, web-like forms that give the technique its name, which means spider. Nui shibori uses running stitches drawn tight before dyeing, and it allows fine control over line and outline. Variations include mokume, which resembles wood grain, and yuki, which resembles snow-covered shapes. Arashi shibori, meaning storm, involves wrapping cloth around a pole, then compressing it and dyeing it, which creates diagonal, rain-like streaks. Itajime shibori folds the cloth into regular shapes and clamps it between boards or blocks, leaving geometric motifs where dye is blocked.

Other Japanese Resist Methods

Shibori is only one part of a wider Japanese tradition of resist dyeing. Rōketsu-zome uses wax as a resist. Katazome employs a paste made from rice, applied through a stencil cut from treated paper, and the pasted areas remain undyed when the fabric is immersed or brushed with color. Tsutsugaki involves drawing freehand lines of rice paste through a cone-shaped tube, much as one would pipe icing; this method has been used for bedding covers, banners, and festival cloths. Yūzen, developed in Kyoto, uses fine paste outlines to separate areas of painted color, and it is closely associated with kimono decoration. Kasuri, a related but distinct technique, resists dye at the thread stage, so that bound yarns are dyed before weaving and form slightly blurred patterns in the finished cloth.

Dyes and Materials

Indigo has long been the dye most closely associated with shibori. Japanese indigo, prepared through fermentation, is applied in repeated dips, and the cloth oxidizes from yellowish green to blue on exposure to air. Cotton, hemp, silk, and later synthetic fibers have all been used. Other dyes, such as madder, safflower, and gromwell, have produced reds and purples, particularly on silk.

Continuity and Revival

Industrial printing and changing dress habits reduced demand for hand-dyed cloth during the twentieth century, and many workshops closed. Preservation efforts, museum collections, and craft associations have since helped sustain the knowledge. Contemporary textile artists and designers in Japan and elsewhere have adapted shibori for fashion, interior fabrics, and sculptural work, and the term is now used internationally, often alongside comparable methods such as bandhani in India and plangi in Indonesia.

title: Bandhani, Leheriya, and Tie-Dye Traditions
text:
Bandhani, Leheriya, and Tie-Dye Traditions

Tie-dyeing is a family of resist-dyeing methods in which parts of a cloth are bound, knotted, stitched, or folded before it is immersed in dye. The bound areas resist the colour, and when the ties are removed, a pattern remains in the undyed or lightly dyed cloth. Versions of the technique appear in South Asia, East Asia, Southeast Asia, West Africa, and Latin America. Two of the best documented are bandhani and leheriya, both associated with western India.

Bandhani

The name bandhani is related to a Sanskrit root meaning "to tie." The craft is practised mainly in Gujarat and Rajasthan, with important centres in Kutch, Jamnagar, and Jaipur. It is also found in parts of Sindh in Pakistan, where related cloths are made. Bandhani is worked on fine cotton, silk, or georgette. The maker pinches up a small portion of the fabric and wraps it tightly with thread, so that each tiny bound point resists the dye. Repeated across the cloth, these points build dots, which are arranged into lines, waves, squares, flowers, birds, and other motifs.

The work is usually done by women, who often tie the cloth with a fingernail, sometimes grown long for the purpose. The tying is then followed by dyeing in stages, from the lightest colour to the darkest. Between stages, additional areas may be tied so that earlier colours are preserved. When the final dyeing is complete, the threads are removed, and the cloth is stretched to reveal a surface of small raised dots, each surrounded by a ring of colour.

Traditional palettes use red, yellow, green, black, and indigo. Natural dyes such as madder, indigo, and pomegranate rind were used historically, although synthetic dyes are now common. Bandhani is closely linked to marriage and other life events. Red and maroon cloths, often with a pattern called a gharchola, are worn by brides in some communities, and yellow is associated with auspicious occasions. Different communities, including Khatri, Muslim, and Kutchi groups, have developed distinct motifs and colour preferences. Some bandhani production has historically been connected with the dyers' trade in Khambhat and Jamnagar, where water quality and local skill were said to affect the colours.

Leheriya

Leheriya, from a word for "wave," is a Rajasthani form of tie-dye that creates diagonal stripes. Instead of tying individual points, the maker rolls a length of cloth diagonally from one corner to the opposite corner. The roll is bound with thread at intervals and dyed. Each dyeing is followed by retying at new places, so that bands of different colours emerge. When the cloth is opened, it shows rippling lines in several colours.

Leheriya is traditionally worn as a turban cloth and as a scarf or veil. It is associated with the monsoon season and with festivals such as Teej, when its colours are considered fitting for the rains. A variant called mothra, produced by tying the cloth in a second direction, gives a checked pattern of small squares. Jaipur, Jodhpur, and Udaipur have long been known for these cloths.

Other Tie-Dye Traditions

Beyond India, tie-dye has many regional forms. In Japan, shibori covers a wide range of resist techniques, including binding, stitching, folding, and clamping. Arimatsu and Narumi in central Japan are known for such work, often in indigo. In West Africa, the Yoruba of Nigeria make adire, in which raffia ties and stitching resist indigo on cotton. Related practices exist in Senegal, Mali, and elsewhere. In Indonesia, the technique called pelangi, or "rainbow," uses ties and stitching on cloth for festive wear. In Peru and Bolivia, pre-Columbian textiles show tied-resist patterns, indicating a long history in the Andes.

Contemporary Practice

Today, bandhani and leheriya are made both for local use and for wider markets. Craftspeople face competition from printed imitations that copy tie-dye designs. Cooperatives, design institutions, and geographical indication protections have been used to support makers and to distinguish handmade work. Interest in natural dyes has also grown, encouraging a return to older methods alongside modern techniques.

title: Block Printing: Ajrakh, Kalamkari, and Beyond
text:
Block Printing: Ajrakh, Kalamkari, and Beyond

Block printing is one of the oldest methods of applying pattern to cloth. A design is carved in relief into a block, usually of wood, and the raised surface is coated with dye, mordant, or resist paste and pressed onto fabric. Repeated impressions build up borders, fields, and all-over patterns. The technique is valued for its speed relative to hand painting and for the distinctive slight irregularities that mark work done by hand. It has been practised across South Asia, East Asia, West Africa, the Middle East, and Europe, and it is closely tied to the availability of natural dyes and to long-distance textile trade.

Block makers

The block carver is a specialist whose work is separate from that of the printer. Seasoned hardwoods such as teak or sheesham are commonly used in India. Fine details are cut with chisels, and brass strips or pins are sometimes set into the wood to render delicate lines. Many blocks are made in sets, with one block for each stage of colour, so that the outlines and fills of a design align when printed in sequence. Blocks are often passed down within workshops and may remain in use for generations.

Ajrakh

Ajrakh is a resist-and-mordant printed cloth associated with Sindh in present-day Pakistan and with Kutch and the Barmer region in western India. It is traditionally worn and used by pastoral and farming communities, as turbans, shawls, and wrappers, and the Khatri printing families have been its best-known makers. Ajrakh is characterised by dense geometric lattices, stars, and floral motifs, most often in deep indigo and madder red, with accents of black and areas of undyed white. The cloth is printed on both sides, so that the pattern appears complete from either face.

The process is long and involves many stages of washing, printing, dyeing, and drying. The fabric is first washed and treated to prepare it to receive dye. A resist paste, commonly made from lime and gum, is printed to protect areas from indigo. Mordants such as iron solutions and alum-based pastes are then printed, and the cloth is dyed in madder or other plant materials, which produce different colours depending on the mordant. Indigo vat dyeing follows, and a final boiling and washing reveal the finished design. Some contemporary workshops have moved to rivers and open ground suited to large-scale washing, since the process depends on abundant clean water.

Kalamkari

The word kalamkari, from "kalam" (pen) and "kari" (work), refers to painted and printed cotton from Andhra Pradesh and neighbouring regions of southern India. Two traditions are generally distinguished. In Srikalahasti, artists draw and paint freehand with a bamboo pen, and the cloth has long been used for temple hangings that depict episodes from Hindu epics and narrative scenes. In Machilipatnam, block printing is combined with hand-applied resists and mordants, and the output has historically included floral hangings, coverlets, and export cloth.

Preparation is central to the craft. Cotton is soaked in a mixture that often includes myrobalan and milk, which helps the fabric hold dye and keeps lines from spreading. Black is made from fermented iron, red from madder with an alum mordant, and blue from indigo. Yellows come from plants such as pomegranate rind or myrobalan. Painted and printed cottons from the Coromandel coast were highly sought in Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and Europe, and they influenced the European chintz fashions of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.

Related traditions

Many other regions have developed block printing in distinct ways. In Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh, dabu printing uses a mud resist, and Bagh printing is known for its red and black palette. Sanganer and Bagru are well-known printing centres. In Indonesia, copper stamps called cap are used to apply wax in batik. In Ghana, Adinkra cloth is stamped with symbolic motifs using carved calabash pieces and a dark dye. In Iran, qalamkar printing has been associated with Isfahan. In France, the toile de Jouy tradition developed from copperplate and block printing in the later eighteenth century.

Contemporary practice

Block printing faces competition from screen and digital printing, as well as concern over water use and effluent. Organisations and craftspeople have responded through geographical-indication protection, training programmes, and renewed interest in natural dyes. Many printers now supply designers and textile conservators as well as local markets.

title: Mud Cloth and Earth Pigments
text:
Mud Cloth and Earth Pigments

Mud cloth is the common English name for a group of textiles decorated with fermented mud and plant-based dyes. The best-known example is bogolanfini, made by the Bamana (Bambara) people of Mali. The Bamana term is usually translated as "mud cloth" or "cloth made with mud". Similar techniques are found among neighbouring peoples in West Africa, and related uses of clay and mineral pigments appear in textile traditions in South Asia and the Pacific.

Cloth and preparation

Traditional bogolanfini begins with cotton that has been spun and woven by men on a narrow strip loom. The strips are sewn edge to edge to form a wider rectangle. Dyeing and painting have generally been women's work, and knowledge of the process is passed from older women to younger relatives.

The cloth is first soaked in a bath made from the leaves and twigs of certain trees, most often a local species of Anogeissus known as n'gallama. This bath is rich in tannins and gives the cotton a pale yellow colour. It also prepares the fibre to react with the mud applied later. The cloth is then dried in the sun.

The mud itself is gathered from riverbeds or ponds, and the preferred sources are often kept within families. It is stored in clay vessels and left to ferment for a long time, sometimes for many months, until it becomes dark, fine and rich in iron compounds. The exact qualities of a batch influence the final depth of colour, and makers regard its preparation as a skill in its own right.

Painting and finishing

The artist applies the mud with a thin piece of metal, a stick or a similar tool. In the classic method, she paints the background around the motifs rather than the motifs themselves, so the design emerges as the yellow ground showing between areas of dark mud. Layers are built up in stages and dried between applications. The iron in the mud combines with the tannins in the cloth to form a lasting black or deep brown.

When the painting is finished, the cloth is washed to remove surplus mud. The yellow areas are then treated with a caustic agent, traditionally a substance made from plant ash or soap, which lightens them to a creamy white. The result is a cloth of dark brown or black patterns against a pale ground. Variations in which the colours are reversed also exist.

Meaning and use

Bogolanfini patterns are rarely purely decorative. Many carry names that refer to plants, animals, tools, historical events, proverbs or social values, and a knowledgeable viewer can read a cloth in part through its motifs. Particular cloths have been associated with life events and protective purposes. Hunters' tunics were made with the belief that they offered protection, and wraps were worn by women during initiation and after childbirth. The dark colour and the earth from which it came were linked to ideas of strength and renewal.

Revival and wider recognition

During the twentieth century, imported fabrics and changing fashions reduced the everyday use of mud cloth. From the 1970s, however, Malian artists and designers began to promote it as a symbol of national and cultural identity. Workshops and artist groups developed new formats, including wall hangings, garments and furnishings, and the cloth gained attention in international fashion and design. This expansion also led to commercial imitations, including printed fabrics that mimic the appearance without the mud process.

Related earth-pigment traditions

Mud and clay are used in other textile crafts. In the Senufo region of northern Côte d'Ivoire, painted cloths known as Korhogo cloth carry figurative scenes drawn in dark pigments on cotton. In Rajasthan and Gujarat in India, the block-printing tradition called ajrakh uses a resist paste called dabu, made from clay, lime and gum, which protects parts of the cloth during dyeing in indigo and madder. In Fiji and elsewhere in Polynesia, barkcloth known as masi or tapa is decorated with pigments made from soot, clays and plant extracts. In each case, local earth and plant materials are used for their chemical properties as well as their colour.

title: Fundamental Embroidery Stitches
text:
Fundamental Embroidery Stitches

Although embroidery traditions differ widely in motif, material and purpose, most of them draw on a relatively small group of basic stitches. These stitches are generally classified by the way the thread lies on or passes through the fabric. Common groupings include flat stitches, linear or outline stitches, looped stitches, knotted stitches and stitches that secure a laid thread. Many regional styles are distinguished less by unusual stitches than by the particular combinations, scale and colour in which familiar stitches are used.

Running Stitch and Its Relatives

Running stitch is the simplest form of embroidery and of sewing. The needle passes in and out of the cloth at regular intervals, leaving a broken line of thread on the surface. It is used for outlines, for quilting and for functional seams, and it underlies several decorative traditions. Japanese sashiko uses rows of running stitches, often in white thread on indigo-dyed cloth, to reinforce and ornament garments. In Bengal and neighbouring regions, kantha work uses running stitches to join layers of old cloth and to create rippled textures and figurative patterns.

Backstitch is worked by returning the needle to the end of the previous stitch, producing a continuous, solid line. It is valued for lettering, fine outlines and detail, and it is the foundation of blackwork, in which geometric fillings are built up in dark thread on light linen. Stem stitch, in which each stitch slightly overlaps the last, gives a twisted, rope-like line that suits curved stems and contours. Split stitch, in which the needle pierces the thread of the preceding stitch, makes a fine line that was widely used in medieval ecclesiastical embroidery to outline and fill small areas.

Flat Filling Stitches

Satin stitch consists of parallel stitches laid closely together so that the ground fabric is hidden and the surface appears smooth and lustrous. It is used in many traditions, including Chinese silk embroidery, Hungarian and Eastern European folk work and Indian regional styles. Because long stitches may snag or loosen, designers often limit the length of satin areas or pad them with a layer of underlying stitches to raise the form. Long and short stitch is a related technique in which stitches of uneven length are staggered in rows, allowing colours to be blended gradually. It is characteristic of the shaded, painterly effects found in Western needlepainting and in some East Asian work.

Looped and Chain Stitches

Chain stitch forms a series of linked loops that resemble the links of a chain. It is one of the oldest known embroidery stitches and appears in textiles from Asia and Europe over many centuries. It can be worked with a needle or, in some traditions, with a hooked tool, as in the ari work of Kashmir and the tambour embroidery used in European and Indian workshops. Blanket stitch and buttonhole stitch are looped stitches worked along an edge, where they protect the fabric from fraying and give a decorative border. Feather stitch, a looped stitch that branches alternately to either side, is often used for vines and for ornamenting seams, as in crazy quilting.

Knots and Laid Work

French knots and related knotted stitches are made by winding the thread around the needle before returning it to the fabric, creating small raised points. They add texture to flowers, eyes and filling areas. Couching is a method in which a thread, or a group of threads, is laid on the surface and held in place by small stitches of a second thread. Because the laid thread does not pass repeatedly through the cloth, couching is well suited to costly materials such as gold and silver wire, and it features prominently in metal-thread embroidery in the Middle East, South Asia and Europe.

Counted-Thread Stitches

Cross-stitch and related techniques are worked by counting the threads of an evenly woven ground, so that each stitch sits in a regular grid. Cross-stitch, in which diagonal stitches intersect, is widespread in European folk costume and in the sampler tradition, where stitchers recorded alphabets and patterns. Other counted techniques, such as Hardanger work from Norway, combine satin-stitch blocks with cut and drawn threads to create open lacelike grounds. In these methods the weave of the cloth acts as a guide, and the character of the finished piece depends closely on the fabric chosen.

title: Whitework, Cutwork, and Drawn Thread
text:
Whitework, Cutwork, and Drawn Thread

Whitework is the broad name for embroidery in which white thread is worked on a white or near-white ground, usually linen, cotton, or fine muslin. Because colour is absent, the effect depends on texture, the play of light across raised and recessed areas, and the contrast between solid stitching and open space. Many whitework traditions overlap with two related techniques, cutwork and drawn thread, which alter the structure of the fabric itself instead of simply decorating its surface.

Drawn thread work

In drawn thread work, selected warp or weft threads are withdrawn from an evenly woven cloth, leaving open channels or panels. The remaining threads are then gathered, bound, or wrapped into patterns, most often with needle-woven stitches that secure the groups in place. The simplest form is hemstitching, in which a row of threads is removed and the threads left behind are bundled just above a hem. More elaborate versions combine many withdrawn bands to form lattices and borders. The method depends on the regularity of the weave, so it has long been associated with household linen such as tablecloths, bed coverings, towels, and church textiles. Related practices are found in Scandinavia, central and eastern Europe, Mexico, and the Mediterranean, where they are often tied to regional costume or to ceremonial cloths.

Cutwork

Cutwork goes a step further by cutting away areas of the ground cloth. To prevent fraying, the edges of each opening are first outlined with close buttonhole stitch or a similar firm edging. In some forms, delicate bars or bridges are worked across the openings to link the remaining solid areas. These are sometimes called brides or bars. Richelieu work, traditionally named after a French cardinal, uses such bars and fairly simple shapes. Reticella, developed in Italy during the Renaissance, combined cut and drawn fabric with geometric needle-made filling and is often cited as a step toward true needle lace, in which the foundation cloth disappears altogether.

Hardanger, from western Norway, is among the best-known examples that join both approaches. Blocks of satin stitch, called kloster blocks, are worked in a regular pattern; threads between the blocks are then cut and removed, and the remaining strands are wrapped or woven to form open grids and small decorative motifs. Related Danish work, known as Hedebo, developed in a rural region near Copenhagen and combined cutwork with drawn thread and fine linen embroidery.

Other regional traditions

Many regions developed distinctive whitework styles using locally available materials.

- Ayrshire work, from southwestern Scotland in the early nineteenth century, used very fine cotton or linen with delicate padded satin stitch and open filling stitches. It was widely used for christening gowns and baby clothing.
- Mountmellick work, from a Quaker community in Ireland, uses heavy cotton thread on a thick cotton ground. It is noted for naturalistic plant motifs, raised knotted stitches, and knitted or knotted fringes.
- Broderie anglaise, a European style of eyelet embroidery, relies on small pierced holes finished with overcast stitch, often arranged in floral patterns.
- Schwalm whitework, from Hesse in Germany, combines drawn thread, pulled stitches, and openwork on linen, and has traditionally been used in household and ceremonial textiles.
- Chikankari, from the Lucknow region of India, is worked traditionally in white thread on fine muslin or other light cloth. Its repertoire includes shadow work, in which stitches on the back of a sheer fabric produce a soft impression on the front, as well as a range of knotted, pulled, and flat stitches. It has long been linked with court patronage and continues as a living craft.
- In the Philippines, fine embroidery on translucent fibre cloths such as piña, a fabric made from pineapple leaf fibre, includes openwork and cutwork, and is used especially for formal garments.

Materials and continuity

Traditional whitework favours smooth, tightly spun threads, such as linen, cotton, and in some cases silk, which hold their form when pulled or cut. Fine needles and small, sharp scissors are standard tools. Much of the work was historically done by women at home or in small workshops, and it often circulated as a trade good as well as a domestic art. Today it survives through regional guilds, cooperatives, and teaching programmes, and techniques once used for everyday linen are now frequently applied to bridal and heirloom textiles.

title: Crewel and European Wool Embroidery
text:
Crewel and European Wool Embroidery

Crewel embroidery is a form of surface embroidery worked with fine, two-ply wool yarn on a firmly woven ground. The word "crewel" is of uncertain origin, though it has been used in English since the late medieval period to describe loosely twisted worsted yarn. Today the term refers both to the thread and to the style of needlework done with it, which is characterized by flowing, plant-based designs and a varied vocabulary of stitches. Although the technique is most closely associated with England, wool embroidery has a long and independent history across Europe, where wool was among the most readily available fibres for both clothing and household furnishings.

Materials and Tools

Traditional crewel work uses a wool thread that is smooth, slightly springy and not heavily spun, allowing it to pass through the ground fabric without fraying. The ground is typically linen, or a linen and cotton twill, which is strong enough to carry the weight of dense wool stitching without puckering. Historically, wools were dyed with natural colourants such as madder for reds, weld for yellows and indigo or woad for blues. Greens were commonly obtained by overdyeing blue with yellow. Many surviving pieces show a characteristic range of muted blues and greens, as the more fugitive dyes have faded over time. Embroiderers generally work with a sharp-pointed crewel needle with a long eye, and stretch the fabric on a frame or hoop to keep the tension even.

Design and Stitches

Classic crewel designs show branching vines, leaves, flowers, birds and animals, often growing from a small mound of ground at the base. The motifs drew on imported printed and painted cottons from India, as well as on herbals, pattern books and Tudor and Stuart decorative traditions. The resulting "Tree of Life" pattern became especially popular for bed hangings and curtains in seventeenth-century England and in the English colonies of North America.

A range of stitches is used to fill and outline shapes. Common examples include:

- Stem stitch, used for lines, vines and outlines.
- Satin stitch, which covers small areas smoothly.
- Long and short stitch, which blends shading within larger forms.
- French knots, which create small raised dots for berries or flower centres.
- Chain stitch and couching, which add texture or secure heavier threads.
- Seeding and trellis fillings, which give variety to leaf interiors.

Part of the appeal of the style lies in this variety. A single leaf may contain several different fillings, giving the surface a lively, textured appearance.

Historical Development

Wool embroidery appears in Europe well before crewel work took its recognizable form. Medieval pieces such as the Bayeux Hanging, which was embroidered with wool on linen in the eleventh century, demonstrate early skill in using wool for narrative imagery. In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, crewel work flourished in English households, where it decorated bed curtains, valances, cushions and wall hangings. Much of this work was done by women in domestic settings, though professional workshops also existed.

Interest in the technique declined in the eighteenth century as fashion shifted toward lighter fabrics and finer silk and cotton embroidery. It revived in the later nineteenth century through the Arts and Crafts movement, whose designers valued handwork and looked to older English models. The Royal School of Art Needlework, founded in 1872, and designers such as May Morris encouraged the use of wool and silk in artistic embroidery.

Other European Traditions

Elsewhere in Europe, wool embroidery took distinct regional forms. In Hungary and Transylvania, bold floral motifs were worked in wool on cloth and leather garments. Scandinavian countries developed wool embroidery for folk costume and church textiles, and Scottish and Irish traditions used wool for shawls and furnishings. In parts of Germany and Switzerland, wool was used for counted-thread and tapestry-style work. Related wool-on-canvas techniques, often called needlepoint, produced upholstery and wall coverings across the continent.

Contemporary Practice

Crewel embroidery remains active among hobbyists, textile conservators and embroidery guilds. Modern practitioners use both traditional patterns and new designs, and the technique is also taught as part of historical textile studies. Museum collections, particularly those holding English and colonial American bed hangings, continue to serve as important references for research and revival.

title: Chinese Embroidery Schools
text:
Chinese Embroidery Schools

Embroidery has been practiced in China for many centuries, and over time several regional traditions developed distinct techniques, materials, and visual vocabularies. Four of these are most often grouped together as the principal schools: Su embroidery, Xiang embroidery, Shu embroidery, and Yue embroidery. They are named after the regions in which they arose, and each is associated with a particular character of stitch, color, and subject matter. Other local traditions, including those of minority peoples, are also widely recognized, and the classification into four schools is better understood as a convenient historical framework than as a strict division.

Su Embroidery

Su embroidery originated in the area around Suzhou in Jiangsu Province, a region long known for silk production and for a refined urban culture. It is admired for its fine, even stitching, its delicate gradations of color, and its elegant compositions. Embroiderers use very thin silk threads, which can be split into extremely fine strands, allowing close control over shading. Common subjects include flowers, birds, goldfish, landscapes, and cats. A celebrated specialty is double-sided embroidery, in which a single piece of semi-transparent fabric carries a complete image on both faces, with the thread ends concealed inside the work so that neither side shows knots or loose ends. Su embroidery has been used for garments, fans, and framed pictures, and it is often regarded as a model of precision.

Xiang Embroidery

Xiang embroidery comes from Hunan Province, particularly the area around Changsha. Its development drew on local folk practice and, according to archaeological finds from the region, on a very old tradition of silk decoration. The school is known for painterly effects and a strong sense of volume. Embroiderers often work from paintings and blend colors from dark to light so that a subject appears almost three-dimensional. Animals such as tigers and lions are classic themes, and the texture of fur is rendered by carefully directed stitches. Xiang work often uses a technique of mixing threads of different shades to suggest depth. Traditionally it has also been associated with ink-painting aesthetics, in which empty space and tonal contrast carry part of the meaning.

Shu Embroidery

Shu embroidery, also called Sichuan embroidery, developed in the Chengdu region. Chengdu has been a center of brocade and silk production for a very long time, and the embroidery tradition grew alongside these crafts. Shu embroidery is characterized by tight, neat stitching, bright and harmonious colors, and a large repertoire of stitch types. It was historically used on quilt covers, pillowcases, clothing, shoes, and screens. Typical motifs include flowers, bamboo, pandas, carp, and auspicious symbols. Many works emphasize a soft sheen produced by the careful direction of silk threads, and the practice remained closely tied to everyday domestic use as well as to commercial production.

Yue Embroidery

Yue embroidery refers to the traditions of Guangdong Province, with Guangzhou and the Chaozhou area often mentioned. Compared with the other schools, it is known for bold, rich colors, dense compositions, and the use of gold and silver thread, as well as padded or raised work that gives images a relief-like quality. Subjects often include phoenixes, dragons, peonies, and scenes of festivity. Because Guangdong was an important trading region, the school has a long association with export goods, and its techniques were adapted to suit foreign as well as domestic tastes. Chaozhou embroidery in particular is noted for its heavily raised designs and for decoration used in temples, theatrical costume, and ceremonial settings.

Other Traditions

Beyond the four principal schools, many communities maintain their own embroidery. Peoples such as the Miao, Dong, Yi, and Tibetans produce work with distinct patterns, often applied to clothing, baby carriers, and ritual items. These traditions typically carry meanings tied to family, ancestry, and local belief, and techniques may include counted-thread work, couching, and appliqué. Regional embroidery in northern China has also used bolder, simpler designs on cotton.

Continuity and Recognition

Embroidery in these traditions has been passed down through families, workshops, and in more recent times, specialist schools and research institutes. Several techniques have been recognized in national and international heritage programs, and efforts continue to document methods and train new practitioners.

title: Suzani and Central Asian Embroidery
text:
Suzani and Central Asian Embroidery

Suzani is a family of decorative embroidered textiles made in the oasis towns and cities of Central Asia, particularly in what is now Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and neighbouring regions. The name comes from the Persian word suzan, meaning needle. Suzani are typically large panels of cotton or silk cloth covered in bold needlework, and they have long been used as wall hangings, bed covers, canopies, and prayer cloths. Although the surviving examples date mostly from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, the tradition is understood to be considerably older and to have developed within the urban and courtly cultures of the Silk Road.

Social Role and Function

Suzani have traditionally been tied to domestic life and to marriage. In many communities, a bride's female relatives began preparing embroidered panels well before the wedding, and the finished pieces formed part of the dowry. They were displayed in the new household, often during the ceremony itself, and were used to decorate the marital chamber. Suzani were also made to mark births and other family events. The work was generally done by women, often in groups, with mothers, daughters, and neighbours each contributing sections that were later joined together.

Construction and Technique

A suzani is usually made from several strips of plain cloth sewn side by side. A specialist designer, known in some regions as a kalamkash, drew the pattern on the cloth in ink or charcoal, after which the strips were separated and distributed among the embroiderers. Once each section was stitched, the strips were reassembled, and the seams were often concealed by the embroidery's continuous motifs.

Several stitches are characteristic of the craft:

- Couching, in which a thread is laid on the surface and held down by small stitches. In Central Asian work this is often called basma, and it produces a smooth, dense, slightly raised surface.
- Chain stitch, commonly worked with a hooked tool similar to an awl, which allows rapid and even lines.
- Satin stitch and buttonhole stitch, used for filling shapes and for outlines.

Silk thread was traditionally dyed with natural materials. Madder gave a range of reds, indigo provided blues, and pomegranate rind and other plant sources contributed yellows and browns. Later, synthetic dyes became common, which changed the colour range of many modern pieces.

Motifs and Symbolism

The most recognisable suzani designs feature large discs or rosettes, flowering vines, leaves, and fruits such as pomegranates. The sun and moon, represented by round forms, appear frequently, as do stylised flowers like the tulip, iris, and carnation. Many motifs are associated with fertility, prosperity, protection, and good fortune, though the meanings attributed to them vary by place and are not always well documented. Some pieces include birds, fish, or other creatures, while Islamic traditions of avoiding figural imagery meant that human figures are generally absent.

Regional Styles

Distinct local styles developed in different centres. Bukhara suzani are known for dense couched work, often in a rich, saturated palette on a pale ground. Samarkand pieces commonly feature a large central rosette surrounded by smaller motifs. Tashkent and Nurata examples tend toward lighter, more open compositions, and those from Shakhrisabz are noted for their vivid colour and bold, sweeping forms. In the Fergana Valley, other embroidery traditions flourished alongside suzani. Beyond Uzbekistan, related embroidery was produced by Tajik, Karakalpak, Kyrgyz, and Turkmen communities, each with its own preferred patterns and techniques. Among them, the Turkmen use of geometric designs and the Kyrgyz use of embroidered felt hangings reflect a more nomadic heritage.

Decline and Revival

During the twentieth century, industrial production and changing social conditions reduced the making of embroidery at home, and many older pieces entered museums and private collections abroad. Since the late twentieth century, craft cooperatives, workshops, and cultural organisations have worked to revive traditional methods, train new embroiderers, and support the use of natural dyes. Contemporary suzani are now made both for local use and for international markets, and designers have adapted the traditional motifs for clothing and furnishings.

title: South Asian Embroidery: Kantha, Chikankari, and Phulkari
text:
South Asian Embroidery: Kantha, Chikankari, and Phulkari

Embroidery in South Asia developed in many regional and communal forms, shaped by climate, available cloth, religious practice, court patronage, and domestic custom. Three traditions are especially well documented: kantha from the Bengal region, chikankari from Lucknow, and phulkari from Punjab. Each uses a different approach to stitch, ground fabric, and purpose, and each has been sustained largely by women's work, although commercial production has also involved many male workshop owners, traders, and printers of patterns.

Kantha

Kantha is associated with Bengal, a region now divided between the Indian state of West Bengal and Bangladesh, and with neighbouring areas such as Odisha and Bihar. The word is often connected to a Sanskrit term for rags, and the craft began as a practice of thrift. Worn saris and dhotis were layered, then held together with fine running stitches that gathered the cloth into a soft, slightly rippled surface. The resulting pieces served as quilts, wraps, bedcovers, and covers for books or valuables.

Threads were traditionally drawn from the coloured borders of discarded saris. Over time the stitching became decorative in its own right. The embroidered form known as nakshi kantha ("patterned kantha") includes lotus medallions, trees of life, boats, animals, village scenes, and geometric borders. Motifs were frequently worked from memory or from the maker's own observation rather than from a fixed template. The Bengali poet Jasimuddin popularised the form in his 1929 poem "Nakshi Kanthar Math," which tells a story through the embroidered cloth. In recent decades, cooperatives and non-governmental organisations in both Bangladesh and India have supported kantha makers, and the stitch is now applied to scarves, jackets, and furnishing fabrics as well as quilts.

Chikankari

Chikankari is a white-on-white or tone-on-tone embroidery centred on Lucknow, in Uttar Pradesh. It is traditionally worked on fine, lightweight cotton or muslin, though silk, georgette, and other fabrics are now common. Several origin accounts exist, including stories linking the craft to the Mughal empress Nur Jahan, but historians generally treat these as uncertain. What is clear is that the craft flourished under the Nawabs of Awadh, whose court made Lucknow a centre of fine clothing, and that it remained a mainstay of the city's economy after the decline of court patronage.

The work is notable for the variety of its stitches, which are often grouped into flat stitches, raised stitches, and openwork. A few well-known examples:

- Bakhia, a double-backed or shadow stitch, worked on the reverse so that its colour shows faintly through the cloth.
- Tepchi, a long, simple running stitch used to outline motifs.
- Murri and phanda, small knot-like or bead-like stitches that form flower centres.
- Jali, openwork in which threads are pulled apart rather than cut, producing a delicate net effect.

Production typically involves a division of labour. Designs are carved into wooden blocks and printed onto the cloth with a washable dye. Embroiderers then work the pattern, and finally the cloth is washed to remove the printing marks. Chikankari from Lucknow received a geographical indication registration in 2008, which is intended to protect its place-based identity.

Phulkari

Phulkari, meaning "flower work," belongs to Punjab and is practised on both sides of the India–Pakistan border, as well as in neighbouring regions such as Haryana. It is worked on coarse, hand-spun and hand-woven cotton, usually in shades of red, brown, or blue, with untwisted silk floss. The embroiderer works from the back of the cloth in darning stitches of varying length, so that the long floating threads on the front create a lustrous, geometric pattern. The technique requires a practised eye, as the design is usually counted by the thread rather than drawn.

Phulkari textiles are closely tied to life events. Grandmothers and mothers would begin pieces for a girl's marriage long before it took place. Sub-types include the bagh ("garden"), in which the embroidery covers the whole cloth so densely that the base is hardly visible, and the sainchi, which depicts figures and scenes from village life. The tradition was disrupted by the Partition of 1947, when many families were displaced, but it has been continued by artisans and revived through museum collections, fashion, and government and community programmes.

Shared characteristics

Despite their differences, the three traditions share an emphasis on the hand-stitched surface, an intimate relationship with domestic life, and continuing adaptation to modern markets.

title: Sashiko and Boro: Japanese Stitching and Mending
text:
Sashiko and Boro: Japanese Stitching and Mending

Sashiko and boro are two related traditions of Japanese textile work that grew out of the need to make cloth last. Both rely on simple running stitch worked in cotton or hemp thread, and both developed chiefly among rural and working-class households in the Edo period (1603–1868) and the following decades. Although they are often discussed together, the terms describe different things: sashiko is a stitching technique, while boro refers to textiles that have been repeatedly patched and repaired.

Origins and Social Context

The word sashiko is usually translated as "little stabs" or "small pricks," a reference to the short, even stitches that characterize the technique. Sashiko was first used for practical purposes. Layers of cloth were joined and reinforced with rows of stitches, which made garments warmer and more durable. Farmers, fishermen, and firefighters wore sashiko-quilted jackets and work clothing, since the stitching added thickness and resistance to abrasion.

Cotton was a costly and scarce material in many northern regions of Japan, where the climate was unsuitable for growing it. Commoners were also restricted at various times in the kinds of fabrics and colors they could wear, and were generally limited to hemp and other bast fibers. Cotton scraps, often obtained through trade, were therefore valued, and households kept even very small pieces for reuse. Garments and bedding were mended, layered, and passed down within families.

Boro

The word boro is commonly glossed as "tattered" or "rags." Boro textiles are made of many pieces of fabric, usually indigo-dyed cotton or hemp, which have been stitched over one another across years or generations. A single bedcover or jacket might carry patches from many different periods, giving the surface a dense and irregular structure. The thread used was typically white or pale, which contrasted with the deep blue ground.

Boro is especially associated with the Tohoku region in northern Honshu, where winters are severe and materials were limited. In this setting, extra layers of cloth had a direct practical value. Such items were often not regarded as objects of beauty by their makers. Boro was sometimes associated with poverty, and in the decades of economic growth after the Second World War many examples were discarded. Interest in them as folk art grew later, helped by collectors and researchers who recognized their aesthetic and historical value.

Techniques and Patterns

Sashiko is worked with a long, relatively thick needle and a thread that is not twisted tightly, traditionally of cotton. The stitcher typically makes a row of running stitches by gathering several stitches on the needle before pulling the thread through. Stitches are kept of even length, and the spaces between them are meant to be about the same as the stitches themselves. Practitioners often aim for stitches to meet precisely at the corners and intersections of a pattern, and lines are generally not allowed to cross at a single point in some traditional designs.

Patterns are mostly geometric and are frequently derived from nature or from everyday life. Common motifs include:

- Seigaiha, overlapping concentric arcs that represent waves.
- Asanoha, a hemp-leaf design built from triangles and radiating lines.
- Shippo, interlocking circles often called "seven treasures."
- Kaki-no-hana and other flower-based designs.

Many motifs carry associations of good fortune, protection, or long life, and some were chosen with the wearer's occupation in mind.

Regional Styles

Several regional styles of sashiko developed. Kogin-zashi, from the Tsugaru area of Aomori Prefecture, uses white thread on indigo cloth in counted patterns that follow the weave of the fabric. Hishizashi, from the same region, produces diamond-shaped patterns. Moyozashi, by contrast, consists of long parallel rows of running stitch arranged into larger designs. Each style reflects local materials and household traditions.

Modern Practice

Today sashiko is practiced both as a mending method and as decorative embroidery. Patterns are available as printed templates, and the technique is taught widely in Japan and abroad. Boro has influenced contemporary fashion and design, and historical pieces are held in museum and private collections. Together, the two traditions are often cited as examples of an approach in which repair is considered part of a textile's life rather than a sign of its end.

title: Appliqué and Reverse Appliqué: Molas and Beyond
text:
Appliqué and Reverse Appliqué: Molas and Beyond

Appliqué is the technique of attaching pieces of fabric to a ground cloth to form a design. In its conventional form, shapes are cut out, positioned on the surface, and stitched down along their edges. Reverse appliqué works in the opposite direction. Several layers of cloth are stacked, and the maker cuts through the upper layers to expose the colors beneath. The raw edges are then turned under and sewn down. Both methods turn plain woven cloth into a layered, graphic surface. Both have been used for clothing, ceremonial objects, bedcovers, and banners in many regions.

The Mola of the Guna People

The best-known example of reverse appliqué is the mola, made by Guna women of the San Blas islands and the adjacent mainland coast of Panama, an area called Guna Yala. In the Guna language the word mola refers to cloth or clothing. It came to mean the decorated panels sewn into the front and back of a woman's blouse. Many scholars link the mola to the older Guna practice of painting designs on the body. Women began to transfer such designs to cloth in the late nineteenth century, when trade brought commercially woven cotton in strong, plain colors.

A mola is built from layers of colored cotton, usually in contrasting shades. The maker tacks the layers together and cuts away small areas of the upper layers with fine scissors. She folds the cut edges under with the tip of her needle and secures them with very small, nearly invisible stitches. The cut openings reveal the colors below. Cutting through successive layers produces bands, outlines, and nested forms. Many makers add small pieces of contrasting cloth between layers, or embroider details on top. Fine work depends on the evenness of the cuts and the neatness of the stitching.

Mola imagery changes with time. Early panels favored abstract geometric patterns, often described as labyrinthine. Later panels show birds, fish, plants, and mythological beings. Some depict scenes from daily life, Christian subjects, or events drawn from the news, and a few carry political messages. Makers often fill the background with repeated lines and small motifs, a habit that suits the technique. Molas are also made for sale, and this trade has become an important source of income for many Guna families. It has encouraged new subjects and formats, such as panels sewn into bags and wall hangings.

Appliqué Traditions Elsewhere

Layered cutwork and applied cloth appear in many other textile cultures, often developed independently.

The Hmong of Southeast Asia and southern China make reverse appliqué panels known as paj ntaub, often combined with embroidery. Their patterns are cut and stitched in repeated geometric forms and are used on clothing and ceremonial garments. After many Hmong people resettled in other countries in the late twentieth century, makers also produced story cloths. These pictorial hangings record migration and village life.

In Egypt, tentmakers in a covered market in Cairo make khayamiya. These large appliquéd panels in bold geometric and calligraphic designs were used for festival and funeral tents and are now also made as hangings and cushion covers.

In the Fon kingdom of Dahomey, now in Benin, court appliquérs made banners and cloths that used emblematic figures to represent kings and their deeds. In Ghana, Fante asafo companies made flags in appliqué, with images that often illustrate proverbs and signal rivalry between groups.

In Odisha, India, the town of Pipli is known for brightly colored appliqué used on canopies, umbrellas, and temple decorations linked to the Jagannath cult in Puri. In western India and Pakistan, appliqué is also used on bedcovers and quilts, including the ralli of Sindh, which combines patchwork and appliqué.

In Europe and North America, appliqué developed into a major quilt-making tradition. Examples include the Baltimore album quilts of the mid-nineteenth century and the Hawaiian quilts that Hawaiian quilters have made since the nineteenth century. Hawaiian quilts have large, symmetrical designs cut from a single folded piece of cloth.

Across these traditions, appliqué allows makers to use small pieces of cloth economically. It also gives broad areas of strong color and clear outline.

title: Mirror Work and Embellished Textiles
text:
Mirror Work and Embellished Textiles

Mirror work is a form of surface embellishment in which small pieces of reflective material are attached to cloth by stitching, usually with an embroidered framework that holds each piece in place. It is most closely associated with the Indian subcontinent, particularly the regions of Gujarat, Rajasthan and Sindh, and is also found in parts of Afghanistan, Iran, and Central Asia. Similar techniques that attach small, light-catching objects to fabric appear in many other textile traditions, and together these practices form a broad category of embellished textiles.

Materials and Origins

The reflective elements are known in Hindi and Gujarati by terms such as abhla or shisha. Early examples are generally thought to have been made from thin sheets of mica, which could be cut into small discs. Later, craftspeople used pieces of blown glass that had been silvered on the inside. The glass was shaped into thin bubbles, broken, and trimmed into rounds, squares, or other shapes. Modern workshops often use manufactured mirrored glass or plastic, which is more uniform and less fragile.

The precise origin of the technique is uncertain. Written and pictorial sources suggest that mirrored and jewelled textiles were valued at courts in South and Central Asia from at least the period of the Mughal Empire, which began in the sixteenth century. Over time the technique spread from courtly circles into the dress and household furnishings of pastoral and farming communities, where it took on local forms and meanings.

Technique

In the usual method, the worker first lays a small mirror against the cloth and anchors it with a foundation of crossed threads. These threads form a lattice over the face of the mirror, leaving the center exposed. The worker then stitches around the edge with buttonhole or blanket stitch, working through the foundation threads and the fabric so that the mirror is held firmly. Finally, the surrounding area is often filled with chain stitch, herringbone stitch, or satin stitch, which turns the mirror into the center of a flower, sun, or geometric motif.

The result depends heavily on the stitcher's regional style. Communities such as the Rabari, Ahir, and Kutchi Jat in Kutch are known for dense compositions in which mirrors are combined with brightly colored silk floss. In Rajasthan, mirrors are often paired with appliqué and block-printed or tie-dyed cloth. In Sindh, mirror work appears alongside fine geometric embroidery on garments for women and on ceremonial textiles.

Related Embellishment Traditions

Mirror work belongs to a larger family of techniques that add small objects or metallic elements to cloth. These include:

- Metal-thread embroidery, such as zardozi, in which gold or silver wire, spangles, and beads are couched on silk, velvet, or other rich fabrics.
- Beadwork, found in many regions, including southern Africa, where beaded cloth and garments carry social and ceremonial significance, and among Indigenous peoples of North America.
- Sequin and spangle work, used in dance costume and festival dress across Asia, Africa, and Europe.
- Shell and coin attachments, used in garments from Central Asia, parts of Southeast Asia, and the Himalayan region.
- Feather and seed decoration, practiced in the Americas and the Pacific.

Cultural Significance

In many communities embellished textiles mark important occasions. Mirror-worked dowry textiles, wall hangings, and animal trappings are made for weddings and festivals. Reflective surfaces are often understood as protective, deflecting the harmful gaze of the evil eye, though interpretations differ between groups. Garments and hangings may also signal the wearer's community, age, and marital status.

Contemporary Practice

Today, mirror work is made both for local use and for wider markets. Cooperatives and design organizations have worked with embroiderers to sustain income and to document traditional patterns. At the same time, the use of machine-made imitations and inexpensive materials has raised concerns about the continuity of hand skills. Conservators and museums also face challenges, since mirrors can detach, glass can degrade, and metal elements can tarnish, making the care of embellished textiles a specialized task.

title: Beadwork and Quillwork on Cloth and Hide
text:
Beadwork and Quillwork on Cloth and Hide

Beadwork and quillwork are surface-decoration crafts in which small, hard elements are attached to a flexible ground such as tanned hide, woven cloth, or bark. Unlike weaving or embroidery with continuous thread, the decorative units are discrete: a flattened porcupine quill, a length of bird quill, a glass bead, or a bit of shell. The designs are built up unit by unit. The two crafts are most closely associated with Indigenous peoples of North America, though beadwork has equally deep roots in parts of Africa, Europe, Asia, and Mesoamerica.

Quillwork

Porcupine quillwork is among the oldest forms of decoration in northern North America and predates the arrival of European trade goods. Quills were gathered, sorted by size, and cleaned. They were then dyed with plant, lichen, and mineral colorants, and later with commercial aniline dyes. Before use they were softened with moisture and flattened, traditionally by drawing them between the teeth or the fingernails.

Several techniques developed. Quills could be wrapped around thongs or fringes, folded and stitched down in rows, plaited into bands, or woven on a simple loom. They were also stitched to birch bark, which was used for boxes and containers in the Great Lakes region and farther east. On hide, quilled bands decorated shirts, moccasins, pipe bags, cradles, and robes. Among many Plains peoples, quillwork was organized through women's societies. Membership could require training, and the right to make certain designs was sometimes held formally.

Glass Beads and the Transformation of Design

Glass beads reached North America through European trade, and by the nineteenth century they were widely available. Larger "pony beads" were followed by finer seed beads, mainly from Venetian and Bohemian workshops. The smaller beads allowed finer curves and more detailed patterns. Beads were sewn with sinew and later with cotton or linen thread, and they gradually displaced quills in much of the continent. Quillwork was often retained for specific ceremonial or conservative uses.

Trade cloth also changed the ground on which decoration was placed. Wool stroud cloth, velvet, and silk ribbon were sewn into garments and then embellished with beads. Ribbon appliqué developed alongside beadwork in several regions.

Principal Techniques

- Lazy stitch (lane stitch): rows of beads are strung and stitched down at intervals, producing a slightly ridged surface. It is closely associated with Plains hide work.
- Overlay or spot stitch: beads are strung on one thread and tacked down by a second thread. This allows curving lines and is well suited to floral designs.
- Loom weaving: beads are woven on a frame into narrow bands, which are then sewn to garments or bags.
- Netting and peyote stitch: beads are joined to one another by thread without any backing, producing fringes, edgings, and covered objects.
- Raised beadwork: beads are strung tightly so that they stand up from the surface, a style associated with Haudenosaunee makers.

Regional Traditions

Plains beadwork is known for bold geometric fields, often on moccasins, bags, and dresses. Great Lakes and eastern peoples favored curving floral and vine motifs, often worked on dark cloth. The Métis of the northern plains became known for floral work, and have sometimes been called the Flower Beadwork People. Subarctic communities combined beadwork, silk embroidery, and moose-hair embroidery, the last of which uses dyed hair in much the same way as quills.

Beadwork Beyond North America

In southern Africa, Zulu and related beadwork is organized around color-coded patterns, and beaded pieces serve as personal ornament and as gifts between people. Interpretations of the colors vary by region and by maker. Ndebele women create beaded aprons and marriage garments. Maasai women make wide collars and ornaments whose colors and layouts signal age and social status. In Yoruba-speaking regions of West Africa, beaded crowns with veils of beads express the sacred authority of kings. In eastern Europe, beaded collars and necklaces, such as the Ukrainian gerdan, form part of regional dress.

Continuity and Revival

Beadwork and quillwork have remained active practices. Many contemporary makers work in older styles for use in ceremony and family life, while others use the techniques in new forms, including jewelry and gallery art. Museum collections and community-led teaching have supported the transmission of regional designs and the study of historical pieces.

title: Scandinavian Embroidery: Hardanger and Blackwork
text:
Scandinavian Embroidery: Hardanger and Blackwork

Embroidery in the Nordic countries has long been shaped by the climate, by the importance of linen and wool in household economies, and by the role of needlework in regional dress. Two techniques are often discussed together in modern needlework literature: Hardanger, which has a clear Norwegian origin, and blackwork, which is a monochrome counted-thread style with a wider European history. The two share an emphasis on precise counting, restrained colour and geometric pattern.

Hardanger

Hardanger embroidery takes its name from the Hardanger district of western Norway, where it developed in rural communities and became closely tied to local costume. It is a form of whitework, traditionally worked in white or undyed thread on white or natural evenweave linen. Its effect depends on texture and on the play of light across solid and open areas, not on colour.

The technique combines several operations. Blocks of straight satin stitches, known in Norwegian as kloster blocks, are worked in repeating geometric arrangements, commonly stepped or diamond-shaped. Once these blocks are complete, the fabric threads that lie within the outlined areas are cut and withdrawn. The remaining threads are then reinforced with woven bars or wrapped bundles, and sometimes decorated with small knotted loops called picots. Filling stitches, including the one known as dove's eye, add lacy detail to the openings. Because the cutting must be done after the edges are secured, the work demands careful planning and a steady hand.

Traditionally Hardanger was used for the aprons, collars, cuffs, bonnets and chemise details of women's regional costume, which in Norway is called the bunad. It also decorated household linens such as tablecloths, runners and bed furnishings. Many scholars suggest that the technique reflects older influences from cutwork and drawn-thread traditions elsewhere in Europe, possibly reaching Norway through trade and through Italian and other continental lace-making. A closely related tradition, Hedebo embroidery, developed in Denmark, and it shares the use of cut and drawn work, although its stitch vocabulary and motifs differ.

During the nineteenth century, Hardanger work was promoted by craft associations that sought to preserve rural handwork as a national cultural expression. Emigrants carried the technique to North America, where it became popular in the twentieth century and is now widely taught through guilds, clubs and printed pattern books. Modern practitioners work on cotton and linen and may use coloured or variegated threads, although white on white remains the classic form.

Blackwork

Blackwork is worked in black thread, historically silk, on white or pale linen. Its patterns are built from small, regular stitches, usually in double running stitch or backstitch, so that both sides of the fabric appear alike. Designers vary the density of the pattern to create areas of light and shade, which allows a flat design to suggest modelling without using more than one colour.

The style is generally associated with Spain and with England, where it was used on sleeves, collars and cuffs in the sixteenth century. It was therefore not an indigenous Scandinavian technique in the way Hardanger is. Its inclusion in Nordic needlework reflects later adoption. Monochrome counted work suited the Scandinavian preference for clear geometry, and designers in the region have used blackwork-like fillings in contemporary pieces. Some use traditional Nordic motifs, such as stars, stylised plants and borders, in place of the older English and Iberian patterns.

Comparison and Continuing Practice

Hardanger and blackwork differ in structure, since one removes threads from the ground and the other builds pattern on its surface. Both, however, rely on evenweave fabric, on counted thread placement, and on a disciplined limited palette. Today both are practised as hobby crafts and as elements of design work. Museums, regional craft associations and folk art schools in the Nordic countries continue to teach Hardanger in particular as part of living textile heritage.

title: Lace-Making Traditions
text:
Lace-Making Traditions

Lace is an openwork textile in which threads are looped, twisted, plaited or stitched into patterned structures, often with open spaces forming part of the design. Unlike woven cloth, true lace does not depend on a regular grid of warp and weft. Instead, the maker builds the fabric thread by thread, either on a supporting pattern or directly in the air. Lace-making developed in several regions of Europe in the sixteenth century and later spread, through trade, migration and missionary teaching, to many other parts of the world. Its traditions are commonly divided into two broad families: needle lace and bobbin lace, with a number of related techniques that use hooks, shuttles or netting.

Needle Lace

Needle lace is made with a single needle and thread, using variations of the buttonhole stitch. The maker first outlines a design on parchment or stiff paper, couches a foundation thread along the outline, and then fills the enclosed areas with stitches of different density. The finished lace is cut free from its backing. Venice became renowned for this technique, and varieties such as point de Venise, with its raised, sculptural relief, were prized by courts and churches. French centres, including Alençon and Argentan, developed finer and more regular styles, and their products were closely tied to royal patronage. Other needle lace traditions include Burano in the Venetian lagoon, Spanish and Italian reticella, and the sun-pattern lace known as Nanduti in Paraguay, which is thought to have combined Spanish influence with local design.

Bobbin Lace

Bobbin lace is made by manipulating many threads wound on small weighted bobbins. The lace-maker sets pins into a pricked pattern fixed to a pillow, and crosses and twists the bobbins in set sequences around the pins. Centres of production grew up in Flanders, with Brussels, Bruges and Mechelen each associated with distinctive styles, and in England, where Honiton, Bedfordshire and Midlands laces developed local characteristics. Valenciennes and Chantilly in France, Genoa in Italy, and the Torchon style common across much of Europe are further examples. In central and eastern Europe, towns such as Idrija in Slovenia and Vamberk in the Czech lands maintain bobbin lace schools. In Spain and Portugal, coastal communities have long produced lace, and the technique was carried to Latin America and the Philippines.

Related Techniques

Several other methods fall within the wider field of lace. Tatting uses a shuttle to form knotted rings and chains, and is usually associated with fine edgings. Crochet lace, including Irish crochet, developed in the nineteenth century and provided income for households during periods of hardship. Filet lace is worked on a knotted net ground, which is then embroidered with a darning stitch. Cutwork and drawn-thread work, found in Hardanger embroidery in Norway and in many Mediterranean traditions, create openwork by removing or gathering threads from an existing cloth. Machine-made net, introduced in the early nineteenth century, allowed hand-worked motifs to be applied to a mechanical ground, as in Carrickmacross and Limerick lace in Ireland.

Materials and Social Context

Linen thread was the principal material in early European lace, and its fineness was a point of pride. Cotton, silk, wool and metallic threads were also used, the latter in gold and silver lace for ceremonial dress. Lace-making was frequently a domestic occupation carried out by women and children, and in many regions lace schools taught the craft from a young age. The work was often poorly paid, even when the finished lace commanded high prices at court. Lace served as a marker of status in clothing and church furnishings, and sumptuary laws in several countries attempted to regulate its use.

Decline and Revival

The introduction of machine lace in the nineteenth century reduced demand for handmade work, and many local industries declined. In the twentieth century, museums, guilds and craft organisations began to document patterns and techniques and to support teaching. Lace-making is now practised mainly as a heritage craft and an art form. Contemporary makers apply traditional methods to sculpture, jewellery and fashion, and in 2009 the lace-making of Idrija was included in UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage, reflecting continuing recognition of the craft.

title: Knitting Traditions: Fair Isle, Aran, and Beyond
text:
Knitting Traditions: Fair Isle, Aran, and Beyond

Knitting, the formation of fabric from interlocking loops of yarn worked with needles, developed into a wide range of regional traditions. Unlike weaving, it requires no loom, and the tools are light and easy to carry. This made it well suited to households, seafaring communities and pastoral peoples, who often knitted while walking, tending animals or minding children. The earliest surviving knitted objects, including socks from Egypt, date to the medieval period. From the late Middle Ages knitting spread across Europe, where guilds of hat and stocking knitters were established in several cities. Over the following centuries, distinct local styles emerged, shaped by available fibres, climate, trade and social custom.

Fair Isle and Shetland

Fair Isle is a small island between the Orkney and Shetland archipelagos, and its name has become attached to a style of stranded colourwork. In this technique, two colours are used in any one row, and the unused yarn is carried across the back of the work. The resulting fabric is dense and warm. Traditional designs are built from bands of small repeating motifs, such as crosses, diamonds, stars and the eight-petalled shapes sometimes called "OXO" patterns. Narrow bands are often separated by simple geometric borders. The palette was historically limited to natural sheep shades and a few dyes, including indigo and madder, and later widened with commercial dyes.

Garments were frequently knitted in the round on sets of double-pointed needles. The knitter then cut the tube open to form armholes or a front opening, a method known as steeking, with the cut edges secured by extra stitches. Fair Isle knitwear gained wide popularity in the 1920s, after the Prince of Wales was seen wearing a pullover in the style. Elsewhere in Shetland, knitters became equally well known for lace. Fine shawls were worked from very thin, soft wool in patterns of openwork, and the best were said to be light enough to pass through a wedding ring.

Aran and the Irish Tradition

Aran knitwear is named for the Aran Islands off the west coast of Ireland. It is characterised by heavily textured surfaces made with cables, twisted stitches, diamonds, moss stitch and basket patterns, usually in undyed cream wool. Several stitches are often combined in vertical panels, with a central cable flanked by smaller patterns. Some writers have attributed symbolic meanings to individual stitches, such as the cable for a fisherman's rope. Another popular idea holds that each family had its own pattern so that drowned fishermen could be identified. Textile historians generally regard this second claim as a later romantic invention rather than a documented practice. The Aran sweater in its familiar form appears to have become established during the early twentieth century and was promoted through pattern publications and cottage industries in the middle of that century.

Ganseys and Fishing Communities

Related garments were made around the coasts of Britain and the Channel Islands. The gansey, or guernsey, is a close-fitting pullover knitted from tightly spun worsted wool, often in dark blue. Its firm fabric resisted wind and spray. Patterns, typically confined to the upper body and sometimes the sleeves, varied from one port to another and were combinations of cables, ladders, chevrons and textured stitches. The plain lower body and sleeves could be re-knitted when worn out.

Scandinavia, the Baltic and the Andes

Nordic knitting includes the Norwegian Setesdal cardigan, or lusekofte, with its small dotted "lice" pattern. It also includes the Icelandic lopapeysa, a yoke sweater made with unspun-looking, lightly twisted native wool and a patterned circular yoke that became widespread in the twentieth century. In Sweden, the Bohus Stickning cooperative, founded in 1939, produced elaborate colourwork garments. In Estonia, the Haapsalu shawl is a lace tradition. Latvian and Estonian mittens are known for dense, intricate colour patterns and are historically associated with marriage customs and gift-giving.

In the Andes, knitted caps with earflaps, known as chullos, are worn throughout the region. On Taquile Island in Lake Titicaca, men knit these caps, and their colours and patterns communicate marital status and community role. The Cowichan sweaters of British Columbia, made by Coast Salish knitters, are another distinct tradition, combining European techniques with local motifs.
