title: Principles of Wet Felting
text:
Principles of Wet Felting

Wet felting is the process of transforming loose animal fibre into a dense, coherent fabric by combining moisture, heat, and mechanical agitation. Unlike weaving or knitting, it uses no yarn, thread, or loom. The fabric is created directly from fibre, and its strength comes from the interlocking of countless individual fibres rather than from any planned structure. Wet felting is one of the oldest textile techniques known, and variants of it have been practised across Central Asia, the Middle East, Scandinavia, the Andes, and many other regions.

The Structure of Wool Fibre

The process depends on the physical makeup of wool. Each fibre is covered by an outer layer of overlapping scales, known as the cuticle, which resemble the shingles of a roof. The fibre also has a natural crimp, or waviness, which gives it elasticity. When fibres are wet and warm, the scales lift slightly. Agitation then causes the fibres to migrate and tangle with their neighbours. Because the scales point in one direction, each fibre tends to travel root-first through the mass and cannot easily return. As the fibres lock together, the mass contracts and thickens, a change generally called shrinkage or fulling.

Fibres other than sheep's wool can be felted. Alpaca, camel, goat, yak, and rabbit fibres are used in various traditions, though they differ in how readily they bond. Fine, highly crimped wools felt quickly, while smooth or coarse fibres may need longer working or blending with more responsive types. Plant fibres and many synthetic fibres lack the necessary scale structure and do not felt by themselves, although they can be held within a wool matrix as decorative or structural additions.

The Roles of Moisture, Heat, and Friction

Three conditions work together. Water allows the fibres to swell and relax so that the scales open. Warmth increases this effect and makes the fibres more flexible. Friction, applied by rubbing, rolling, pressing, or beating, drives the movement that produces entanglement.

Many felters add a mild alkaline agent, traditionally a plant-based or animal-fat soap, which raises the pH of the water and helps the scales to open. The soap also lubricates the fibres, allowing them to slide past one another. Some traditions have used other substances, such as fermented liquids or ash-based solutions, for similar purposes. Strongly acidic or very hot conditions can damage the fibre or cause uneven results, so practitioners usually work with warm rather than boiling water.

Layering and Fibre Direction

Felt is typically built from thin layers of carded or combed fibre laid on a flat surface. Each layer is placed with fibres running at right angles to the layer below. This crossing arrangement helps the finished cloth shrink evenly in all directions and reduces the chance of weak points or distortion. Thin, even layers generally give a more consistent result than thick, uneven ones.

Once the fibre is laid out, it is wetted carefully and pressed to expel air. The work then passes through stages that are often described as setting, rubbing, and fulling. In the early stage, the fibres are only lightly attached and the fabric can be pulled apart. As work continues, the surface becomes stable, and the felt can be handled more vigorously. In the final stage, it is rolled, kneaded, or thrown until it reaches the desired firmness and size.

Traditional Methods of Agitation

Methods of applying friction vary by region. In many Central Asian traditions, the wetted fibre is rolled tightly inside a reed mat or cloth and then pulled, pushed, or trampled, sometimes with the roll dragged behind an animal. In other settings, felt is worked by hand on a ridged board or beaten with sticks. Fulling mills, driven by water power, applied the same principle to woven wool cloth in parts of Europe.

Shrinkage and Planning

Because felting contracts the material, makers must anticipate the finished dimensions. Shaped items such as hats, boots, and bags are often made over a resist, a flat or three-dimensional form that prevents the inner surfaces from bonding. After the felt is formed, the resist is removed, leaving a hollow, seamless object. Careful control of shrinkage allows makers to give such objects their final shape while still wet, after which the felt is dried and set.

title: Needle Felting and Modern Techniques
text:
Needle Felting and Modern Techniques

Needle felting, sometimes called dry felting, is a method of consolidating wool fibre into a dense fabric or solid form without water, soap or heat. It differs from the older wet felting traditions of Central Asia, Anatolia and Scandinavia, in which moisture, friction and agitation cause scales on the wool fibres to interlock. In needle felting the same interlocking is produced mechanically, by repeatedly pushing a barbed needle through loose fibre.

Origins and industrial background

The technique grew out of industrial needle-punching, a process developed in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries to make nonwoven fabrics for use in carpet backing, insulation, filters, upholstery and automotive interiors. Machines drive large numbers of barbed needles through a web of loose fibre, tangling the layers together into a coherent sheet. Handcraft needle felting adapted this principle to a single needle or a small group of needles held in a handle. It became widespread among hobbyists and artists in the later twentieth century and has expanded considerably since the early 2000s, helped by the availability of inexpensive tools and online instruction.

Tools and materials

The central tool is the felting needle, a thin steel shaft with small notches, or barbs, cut along its lower end. When the needle is pushed into wool, the barbs catch fibres and carry them deeper; when it is withdrawn, the fibres generally stay in place. Needles differ in thickness, in the shape of their cross-section, and in the arrangement of their barbs. Coarser needles are used to build form quickly, and finer ones to smooth surfaces and add detail. Needles are made of brittle hardened steel and break easily if bent or twisted, and the sharp points require careful handling.

Work is usually carried out on a dense foam pad, a firm brush mat or a block of similar material that absorbs the needle without damaging it. The preferred fibre is typically carded wool in the form of batting, roving or combed top. Breeds with a relatively coarse, crimped fleece felt readily and are often chosen for sculptural work, whereas fine Merino wool suits surface detail and flat pictures. Dyed wool, plant fibres, silk and other materials may be added for colour and texture.

Methods and forms

Needle felting is used in three broad ways. In sculptural work, wool is wrapped or rolled into a loose shape and stabbed repeatedly until it firms. Figures, animals and decorative objects are built up by adding fibre to a core and refining the surface. In two-dimensional work, sometimes described as wool painting, thin layers of coloured fibre are attached to a backing of felt, wool fabric or other cloth to produce pictures or decorative panels. In embellishment, fibre is stitched into existing textiles, including garments, hats, bags and woven pieces, to add pattern or to repair worn areas.

Related contemporary techniques

Needle felting is often combined with other methods. Nuno felting, a term drawn from a Japanese word for cloth, bonds wool fibre to a light fabric such as silk gauze through wet felting, producing a supple material with a textured surface. Needle felting may then be used to add localized details. Embellishing machines, which are domestic adaptations of the industrial needle loom, hold several needles in a head that is moved over the work, allowing designs to be formed quickly on fabric. Wet and dry techniques are also joined in hollow forms, where a wet-felted shell is later sculpted with needles.

Cultural and contemporary significance

Whereas traditional felt-making is often a communal activity tied to particular regions and to practical products such as tents, rugs and clothing, needle felting is generally a small-scale, individual practice. It has been taken up in fine art, soft sculpture, fashion, theatre and puppet making, and in craft education. Some practitioners value it for its use of wool, a renewable natural fibre, and for the possibility of reusing scraps. Others work to connect it with older felting traditions, and many makers combine both approaches, treating the dry technique as an extension of a long history of working with wool rather than a replacement for it.

title: Central Asian Felt: Yurts and Shyrdak
text:
Central Asian Felt: Yurts and Shyrdak

Felt-making has long been central to the material culture of the steppe and mountain regions of Central Asia, where pastoral communities in present-day Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Mongolia, and neighbouring areas have relied on the wool of their sheep for shelter, floor coverings, clothing, and saddlery. Unlike woven cloth, felt is produced by applying moisture, heat, and pressure to loose fibres, which interlock to form a dense, durable fabric. The technique requires no loom and suits the mobile way of life of herding peoples, who have traditionally moved their flocks between seasonal pastures.

The Yurt

The best-known use of felt in the region is the covering of the yurt, a portable dwelling with a collapsible lattice wall, a roof of poles, and a central wooden ring at the crown. The structure is known by different names, including "ger" in Mongolia and "boz üy" in Kyrgyz. Thick sheets of felt are wrapped around the wooden frame and secured with ropes and woven bands. The felt provides insulation against both winter cold and summer heat, and it sheds wind and light rain. Additional layers may be added in colder seasons, and the roof opening can be covered or uncovered to regulate smoke and light.

Felt production for a yurt is traditionally a communal task. Wool is sheared, cleaned, beaten, and spread in even layers over a reed mat or a hide. The layers are dampened with hot water, tightly rolled up with the mat, tied, and then dragged or rolled across the ground, often behind a horse or camel, or worked by groups of women and men kneeling and pressing along its length. The roll is opened and re-rolled several times so that the fibres bond evenly. The finished sheet is then rinsed, shaped, and left to dry. The collective nature of the work has made felt-making an occasion for social gathering, and in many communities it is associated with hospitality and the marking of marriages.

Interior Furnishings

Felt also forms much of the interior of the yurt. Floor carpets, wall hangings, bedding, and storage bags are made from it, and the ornamental treatment of these items is a major vehicle for traditional design. Motifs commonly refer to the natural and pastoral world, with stylised horns, plants, and animal forms recurring across regions. Many designs carry protective or auspicious meanings, though interpretations vary between communities and families.

Shyrdak

Shyrdak is a type of decorated felt carpet especially associated with Kyrgyzstan, though similar work is found in Kazakh communities, where it is often called "syrmak." It is made by a mosaic-like technique. Two sheets of felt in contrasting colours are laid together, and a pattern is drawn on the upper sheet. The pattern is cut out through both layers at once, producing two matching pieces whose shapes are exact negatives of one another. The pieces are then exchanged, so that the cut shapes of one colour fit into the background of the other. This yields two carpets with identical designs in reversed colours.

The pieces are joined by stitching along their edges, and the seams are usually covered with twisted cord, often in a contrasting colour. The carpet is then backed with a further layer of felt or fabric and covered with rows of fine stitching, which both strengthen the piece and add texture. Colours were historically obtained from natural dyes, though synthetic dyes are now widely used. The curling, symmetrical patterns often include horn-like scrolls and geometric borders.

A related Kyrgyz technique, ala kiyiz, involves felting dyed wool directly into the base sheet, so that the design is integral to the fabric rather than cut and applied. In this method, patterned wool is laid out and then pressed and rolled together.

Recognition and Continuity

In recent decades, felt-making has received attention from cultural organisations. In 2012, traditional Kyrgyz felt carpet making was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, and the craft of the yurt has also been recognised in the region. Cooperatives and women's groups now produce felt goods for sale in domestic and international markets, which provides income to rural households while presenting challenges, including the adaptation of traditional motifs to commercial demand.

title: Felt Garments and Hats
text:
Felt Garments and Hats

Felt has been used to make clothing for as long as people have kept wool-bearing animals. Because it is formed by matting fibres rather than spinning and weaving them, felt can be shaped directly into protective garments without cutting and sewing, or with very little of either. This property has made it especially valuable in regions with cold winters, high winds and mobile ways of life, where clothing must insulate, shed moisture and be repaired or replaced from locally available materials.

Central Asia and the Steppe

The most extensive traditions of felt clothing are found across the steppe and mountain regions of Central Asia, Mongolia and the Altai. Archaeological finds from burial sites in the Altai, preserved by frozen ground, include felt boots, stockings, caps and decorated hangings from the first millennium BCE, showing that tailored felt garments were already sophisticated in antiquity. Pointed and rounded felt caps appear in ancient representations of steppe peoples and have long served as markers of identity.

In Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan, the white felt hat known in Kyrgyz as the ak kalpak is a well-known example. Its tall, tapering crown and upturned brim are often decorated with black braid or stitched patterns, and it is worn on formal occasions. The craft was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2012. Felt coats, vests and cloaks are also made in the region. Shepherds' cloaks, cut in a broad, nearly circular form, give protection from rain and snow and can double as bedding.

Mongolian herders wear felt boots with thick soles and turned-up toes, along with hats and linings for the traditional deel, or long coat. Felt is commonly layered with leather, silk or cotton, and the edges of garments are frequently reinforced with stitched bands.

Europe and the Mediterranean

In Europe, felt was long used for rural and occupational clothing before it became associated with fashionable hat making. Shepherds in the Balkans, the Carpathians and parts of the Mediterranean wore felt caps and heavy cloaks. In Turkey, felt cloaks known as kepenek are made by shepherds in Anatolia and are valued for their resistance to rain. In the Pyrenees and Alps, felt hats formed part of regional dress.

Hat making developed into a specialised trade in many European towns from the medieval period onward. Makers used fur fibres, especially beaver and later rabbit, as well as wool. The fibres were formed into a loose cone, hardened with heat, moisture and agitation, and then stretched over wooden blocks to give the required shape. Stiffening agents such as shellac were often applied. The bowler, the top hat and the fedora all derive from this tradition, and felt hat making remains active in a number of European centres.

Other Regions

Felt clothing is also made in the Middle East, the Caucasus and South Asia. In Iran and Afghanistan, felt vests, caps and coats are produced by itinerant and village makers. In the Caucasus, the felt cloak known as the burka became part of the dress of mountain communities and was later adopted by horsemen elsewhere. In parts of North Africa, felted wool hoods and capes appear in pastoral dress.

In the Americas, felt hat making arrived with European settlers and was adapted to local conditions. Wide-brimmed felt hats became linked with ranching and farming life, and regional forms developed in the Andes and Mexico.

Techniques and Decoration

Garments may be felted flat and then cut, or shaped around a resist, a template that allows seamless forms such as boots and hats to be created. Decoration is achieved by laying coloured wool into the surface before felting, by inlaying contrasting layers, or by stitching, braiding and appliqué after the piece is finished. Motifs often carry meanings associated with protection, fertility or clan identity.

Contemporary Practice

Today, felt garments are produced both as everyday items and as heritage crafts. Cooperatives and artisans in several countries work to sustain traditional methods while developing new designs for wider markets, and the continued use of felt in ceremonial dress helps maintain skills across generations.

title: Textile Symbolism, Ritual, and Identity
text:
Textile Symbolism, Ritual, and Identity

In many societies cloth is more than a practical material. Woven, dyed, embroidered, and felted textiles often carry meanings that connect individuals to family, community, ancestors, and the spiritual world. Because making cloth usually involves long periods of skilled labour and the transformation of raw fibre into a finished object, textiles are frequently treated as embodiments of time, knowledge, and social relationships. Anthropologists and art historians have long noted that cloth can serve as a form of record, a medium of exchange, and a statement of belonging.

Pattern and Meaning

Motifs in traditional textiles are often drawn from a shared visual vocabulary that is understood within a particular group. In the Andes, the woven designs of communities around Cusco and in the Bolivian highlands represent mountains, rivers, animals, and agricultural cycles, and the arrangement of pattern bands can signal the village of the wearer. Among the Maya of Guatemala and Chiapas, the designs on huipiles, the traditional blouses, may refer to cosmological ideas such as the layers of the world, the path of the sun, or the sacred maize plant, and a trained observer can often identify a woman's home town from her garment. In West Africa, the Akan of Ghana associate particular kente cloth patterns with proverbs, historical events, and moral qualities, so that the choice of a cloth communicates a message as well as an aesthetic preference.

Colour carries symbolic weight as well. Indigo-dyed cloth is valued across West Africa, South and Southeast Asia, and Japan, and is linked in various places with protection, status, mourning, or fertility. Red, produced from madder, cochineal, or lac, is widely associated with life, blood, and vitality, and appears prominently in wedding textiles from the Balkans to northern India. Interpretations are not universal, however, and the same colour may have different or even opposing meanings in neighbouring cultures.

Ritual and Life Passages

Textiles frequently mark transitions in the human life cycle. Birth blankets, wedding veils, initiation garments, and burial shrouds appear in many traditions. In parts of Indonesia, such as Sumba and Toraja territory, large ceremonial cloths are exchanged between families at marriages and funerals, forming part of a network of obligations. Ikat textiles from the region may be wrapped around the deceased, reflecting a belief that cloth accompanies the person into the afterlife. The ancient burial textiles of the Paracas culture on the southern coast of Peru, dating to the first millennium BCE and the early centuries CE, are among the best-known examples of cloth used in funerary ritual.

Cloth also plays a role in religious practice. Prayer flags in the Himalayas, Shinto ritual cloths in Japan, ceremonial altar cloths in Christian churches, and the kiswa that covers the Kaaba in Mecca each demonstrate how fabric can sanctify a space or an act. Felt is central to the ritual life of many Central Asian peoples; in Kyrgyz and Kazakh households, felt carpets such as the shyrdak and tush kiyiz are made for the home, and the yurt itself is covered in felt, giving the fabric associations of shelter, hospitality, and family continuity.

Identity, Status, and Belonging

Dress and cloth have historically indicated rank, occupation, marital status, and ethnic affiliation. Scottish tartans, though their association with specific clans was largely formalised in the nineteenth century, illustrate how a woven pattern can become a lasting emblem of group identity. In imperial China, the use of particular colours and embroidered symbols, such as the dragon, was restricted by rank. In many communities, rules governing who may weave, who may wear a given cloth, and when it may be worn reinforce social structure.

Textiles can also express resistance and cultural revival. Embroidered garments and tapestries have been used to preserve language, assert land claims, and document experience, as in the pictorial needlework of Hmong refugees and the community arpilleras of Chile. In recent decades, many Indigenous and minority weavers have worked to protect traditional designs from unauthorised commercial copying, raising continuing questions about cultural ownership and the sustainability of handmade traditions.

title: Trade Routes and Cultural Exchange in Textiles
text:
Trade Routes and Cultural Exchange in Textiles

Textiles have been among the most widely traded goods in human history. They are light relative to their value, durable when properly stored, and easily divided into portions for sale. As a result, cloth, fibres, dyestuffs, and the techniques used to work them have travelled across continents for thousands of years, carrying with them motifs, technical knowledge, and ideas about status and belief. Many of the traditions described elsewhere in this article cannot be understood fully without reference to these exchanges.

The Silk Roads

The best known network of textile exchange is the group of overland and maritime routes often called the Silk Roads. Silk production originated in China, and for a long period the methods of raising silkworms and reeling the filament were closely guarded. Silk fabrics moved westward through Central Asia, where oasis cities such as Samarkand and Bukhara became centres of weaving and trade. Over time, sericulture itself spread to Central Asia, Persia, the Byzantine world, and later Italy and other parts of Europe. Traditional accounts attribute the arrival of silkworm eggs in Byzantium to the sixth century.

The routes carried more than silk. Cotton, wool, linen, carpets, and felt were also traded, and dyes such as indigo and madder travelled alongside them. Designs moved with the cloth. Persian and Central Asian patterns, including medallions, palmettes, and paired animals, appear in fabrics produced far from their places of origin, and Chinese weavers in turn adopted motifs from the west.

Indian Ocean and Maritime Exchange

Sea routes across the Indian Ocean connected South Asia, the Arabian Peninsula, East Africa, and Southeast Asia. Cotton textiles from the Indian subcontinent, particularly those decorated with mordant-dyed and resist-dyed patterns, were exchanged for spices and other goods. Fragments of Indian cloth found in Egyptian burial sites and in Indonesian collections show the long reach of this trade. In some Indonesian islands, imported Indian patola cloths became sacred heirlooms, and their geometric designs influenced local weaving and ikat patterns.

Indigo, derived from different plant species in Asia, Africa, and the Americas, became a global commodity. Its cultivation and processing shaped regional economies, and in West Africa the use of indigo-dyed cloth developed into distinctive traditions of strip weaving and pattern dyeing.

Trans-Saharan and African Networks

Caravan routes across the Sahara linked West Africa with North Africa and the Mediterranean. Cloth was itself a form of currency in some regions, with standard lengths of woven strip circulating as a measure of value. Narrow-strip looms, operated mainly by men in many West African societies, produced cloth that was sewn into larger garments, and imported materials such as silk thread were sometimes unravelled and rewoven into local fabrics.

The Americas and Global Trade

Before European contact, Andean and Mesoamerican societies exchanged cotton, camelid fibre, feathers, and dyes such as cochineal over long distances. After the sixteenth century, cochineal became an important export to Europe, where it was valued for its strong reds. Colonial trade also brought sheep to the Americas, leading to new wool-weaving traditions, such as those of the Navajo, which combined older techniques with new materials.

Mechanisms of Exchange

Textile knowledge moved through several channels: the migration of craftspeople, the movement of refugees and conquered populations, diplomatic gifts, pilgrimage, and the activities of merchants. Court workshops often gathered skilled artisans from different regions, encouraging the blending of styles. Embroidery stitches, felting methods, and loom designs frequently spread in this way.

Effects on Local Traditions

Exchange has not been a one-way process of imitation. Communities commonly adapted imported designs to local meanings, reinterpreting foreign motifs within their own symbolic systems. Imported goods could also stimulate new local production, as weavers sought to imitate prized foreign cloths using available materials. In more recent periods, industrial manufacturing and global markets have altered these patterns, both threatening some hand-made traditions and creating new demand for them.

title: Preservation, Conservation, and Revival of Craft Traditions
text:
Preservation, Conservation, and Revival of Craft Traditions

Traditional textile crafts have been shaped by local materials, climate, trade, and social custom, and many are now vulnerable. Industrial production, changing consumer tastes, urban migration, and the loss of older practitioners have all reduced the number of people who weave, dye, embroider, or felt by hand. Efforts to safeguard these crafts fall broadly into three overlapping areas: preserving knowledge and skills, conserving historic objects, and reviving practices that have declined or lapsed.

Safeguarding Living Knowledge

Much textile knowledge is transmitted through apprenticeship, within families, or in community settings rather than through written instruction. For this reason, preservation often focuses on the practitioner rather than the object. Documentation projects record techniques, vocabulary, pattern repertoires, and the social contexts in which cloth is made and used. Photography, film, and oral history are common methods, and many projects aim to return recordings to the communities concerned.

International recognition has played a role. UNESCO's Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, adopted in 2003, allows states to propose living traditions for listing. Several textile practices have been inscribed, including various forms of weaving, embroidery, and felt making. Supporters argue that recognition raises public awareness and can encourage younger people to learn; critics note that listing does not by itself guarantee income or continuity, and that it may sometimes shift how a craft is practiced in order to suit outside expectations.

Some countries operate national schemes that honour master artisans or provide stipends to teachers. Apprenticeship programmes, craft schools, and community workshops try to ensure that skills pass to a new generation, sometimes combining traditional instruction with training in business, design, and marketing.

Conservation of Historic Textiles

Textiles are among the more fragile categories of heritage. Light, humidity, insects, dust, and handling cause fibres to weaken, dyes to fade, and structures to fail. Natural dyes can differ greatly in lightfastness, and some historic mordants, notably iron-based ones, can degrade the fibres they were meant to fix.

Conservators therefore stress preventive measures: controlled lighting, stable temperature and humidity, appropriate storage, and careful display. Large flat textiles may be stored rolled or laid flat, and supported with acid-free materials. Active treatment is generally kept to the minimum necessary. Cleaning, stabilizing weak areas with stitched supports, and reversible repairs are preferred to extensive restoration, in line with widely accepted ethical principles that favour reversibility and documentation of any intervention.

Scientific analysis assists this work. Techniques such as fibre identification and dye analysis can reveal the origin of materials, date a piece, or guide the selection of treatments. Such findings also inform revival efforts by showing how historic colours and structures were achieved.

There are also ethical questions about ownership and display. Many textiles in museum collections were acquired during colonial periods or under unequal conditions, and some communities seek their return or shared stewardship. Sacred or ceremonial cloths may require particular forms of care, which conservators increasingly develop in consultation with source communities.

Revival and Contemporary Practice

Revival movements seek to restore techniques that have fallen out of use. Natural dyeing is a frequent example: researchers and dyers have reconstructed processes using historical recipes and surviving samples, and have re-established cultivation of dye plants. Handloom weaving, regional embroidery styles, and felt traditions have likewise been supported by cooperatives, designers, and non-governmental organizations.

Market-based approaches carry both benefits and risks. Fair-trade arrangements and geographical indications can help makers secure fairer returns and protect regional identity. However, increased demand may encourage imitation, mass-produced copies, or simplified designs, and questions of intellectual property and cultural appropriation remain unresolved in many places.

Successful revival typically depends on maintaining the connection between craft and community. Where makers retain control over design, pricing, and the transmission of skills, traditions tend to adapt while keeping their meaning. Where they do not, the form of the craft may survive while its knowledge and social foundations are lost.

title: tokenizers/whitespace.py — Split text on whitespace runs into simple word tokens
text:
tokenizers/whitespace.py — Split text on whitespace runs into simple word tokens

"""Whitespace tokenizer.

Splits text into word tokens wherever one or more whitespace characters
occur. No attempt is made to separate punctuation from words; a token is
simply a maximal run of non-whitespace characters. For punctuation-aware
splitting, see ``tokenizers.words``.

Typical usage::

    >>> from tokenizers.whitespace import tokenize
    >>> tokenize("  hello   world\n")
    ['hello', 'world']
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import re
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Iterable, Iterator, List, Optional

__all__ = [
    "Token",
    "WhitespaceTokenizer",
    "tokenize",
    "tokenize_with_offsets",
    "count_tokens",
]

# One or more Unicode whitespace characters. The pattern is compiled once at
# import time. ``\s`` in a str pattern covers spaces, tabs, newlines, and
# other Unicode separators recognised by Python's ``str.isspace``.
_WHITESPACE_RUN = re.compile(r"\s+")

# One or more characters that are not whitespace.
_NON_WHITESPACE_RUN = re.compile(r"\S+")


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Token:
    """A token together with its position in the source text.

    Attributes:
        text: The token string.
        start: Index of the first character of the token in the source.
        end: Index just past the last character of the token, so that
            ``source[start:end] == text``.
    """

    text: str
    start: int
    end: int

    def __str__(self) -> str:
        return self.text


class WhitespaceTokenizer:
    """Configurable tokenizer that splits on runs of whitespace.

    Args:
        lowercase: If true, each token is lowercased before being returned.
        max_tokens: If given, stop after this many tokens have been
            produced. ``None`` means no limit.
        keep_empty: Unused by the default pattern, since runs of whitespace
            never yield empty tokens, but accepted so that callers can share
            a common keyword signature across tokenizer classes.
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        lowercase: bool = False,
        max_tokens: Optional[int] = None,
        keep_empty: bool = False,
    ) -> None:
        if max_tokens is not None and max_tokens < 0:
            raise ValueError("max_tokens must be None or non-negative")
        self.lowercase = lowercase
        self.max_tokens = max_tokens
        self.keep_empty = keep_empty

    def iter_tokens(self, text: str) -> Iterator[Token]:
        """Yield ``Token`` objects for each word in ``text``, in order."""
        if not isinstance(text, str):
            raise TypeError(f"expected str, got {type(text).__name__}")

        produced = 0
        for match in _NON_WHITESPACE_RUN.finditer(text):
            if self.max_tokens is not None and produced >= self.max_tokens:
                return
            value = match.group()
            if self.lowercase:
                value = value.lower()
            yield Token(value, match.start(), match.end())
            produced += 1

    def tokenize(self, text: str) -> List[str]:
        """Return the tokens of ``text`` as a list of strings."""
        return [token.text for token in self.iter_tokens(text)]

    def tokenize_many(self, texts: Iterable[str]) -> List[List[str]]:
        """Tokenize each string in ``texts`` and return one list per input."""
        return [self.tokenize(text) for text in texts]


# A shared default instance used by the module-level helpers below.
_DEFAULT = WhitespaceTokenizer()


def tokenize(text: str, lowercase: bool = False) -> List[str]:
    """Split ``text`` on whitespace runs and return the word tokens.

    Leading and trailing whitespace is ignored, and consecutive whitespace
    characters are treated as a single separator.

    >>> tokenize("one  two\tthree")
    ['one', 'two', 'three']
    >>> tokenize("   ")
    []
    >>> tokenize("Mixed CASE", lowercase=True)
    ['mixed', 'case']
    """
    if lowercase:
        return WhitespaceTokenizer(lowercase=True).tokenize(text)
    return _DEFAULT.tokenize(text)


def tokenize_with_offsets(text: str) -> List[Token]:
    """Return ``Token`` objects that record where each word was found.

    >>> [(t.text, t.start, t.end) for t in tokenize_with_offsets("ab  cd")]
    [('ab', 0, 2), ('cd', 4, 6)]
    """
    return list(_DEFAULT.iter_tokens(text))


def count_tokens(text: str) -> int:
    """Return the number of whitespace-separated tokens in ``text``.

    This avoids building a list of strings and is suitable for large inputs.

    >>> count_tokens("a b  c")
    3
    """
    return sum(1 for _ in _NON_WHITESPACE_RUN.finditer(text))

title: tokenizers/regex_tokenizer.py — Configurable regex-based tokenizer with named patterns

tokenizers/regex_tokenizer.py — Configurable regex-based tokenizer with named patterns

"""Configurable regex-based tokenizer.

A RegexTokenizer is built from an ordered list of named patterns. The
patterns are joined into one alternation, so earlier patterns take priority
when several could match at the same position. Each token records the name
of the pattern that produced it, together with its offsets in the source.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import re
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Iterable, Iterator, List, Sequence

__all__ = ["Token", "TokenPattern", "TokenizeError", "RegexTokenizer", "DEFAULT_PATTERNS"]

_NAME_RE = re.compile(r"[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*\Z")
_ERROR_MODES = ("raise", "skip", "emit")


class TokenizeError(ValueError):
    """Raised when no pattern matches and on_error is 'raise'."""

    def __init__(self, text: str, position: int) -> None:
        self.position = position
        snippet = text[position:position + 10]
        super().__init__(f"no pattern matches at offset {position}: {snippet!r}")


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Token:
    """A single token. start is inclusive and end is exclusive."""

    type: str
    text: str
    start: int
    end: int


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class TokenPattern:
    """A named pattern.

    name  -- identifier used as the token type; must be a valid Python name.
    regex -- regular expression source. Capturing groups are allowed, but
             named groups are not, because names are reserved for patterns.
    skip  -- when True, matches are consumed but not yielded.
    """

    name: str
    regex: str
    skip: bool = False


DEFAULT_PATTERNS: Sequence[TokenPattern] = (
    TokenPattern("SPACE", r"\s+", skip=True),
    TokenPattern("NUMBER", r"\d+(?:[.,]\d+)*"),
    TokenPattern("WORD", r"[^\W\d_]+(?:['\u2019-][^\W\d_]+)*"),
    TokenPattern("PUNCT", r"[^\w\s]"),
)


class RegexTokenizer:
    """Split text into tokens using an ordered set of named patterns.

    Example:
        >>> tok = RegexTokenizer()
        >>> [t.text for t in tok.tokenize("Don't panic, 42 times.")]
        ["Don't", 'panic', ',', '42', 'times', '.']

    Parameters:
        patterns -- iterable of TokenPattern; defaults to DEFAULT_PATTERNS.
        flags    -- re flags applied to the combined expression.
        on_error -- what to do with text no pattern matches:
                    'raise' raises TokenizeError,
                    'skip' drops one character and continues,
                    'emit' yields that character as an UNKNOWN token.
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        patterns: Iterable[TokenPattern] = DEFAULT_PATTERNS,
        flags: int = 0,
        on_error: str = "raise",
    ) -> None:
        if on_error not in _ERROR_MODES:
            raise ValueError(f"on_error must be one of {_ERROR_MODES}, got {on_error!r}")
        self._patterns: List[TokenPattern] = list(patterns)
        if not self._patterns:
            raise ValueError("at least one pattern is required")
        self._validate(self._patterns)
        self._skip = frozenset(p.name for p in self._patterns if p.skip)
        self._on_error = on_error
        source = "|".join(f"(?P<{p.name}>{p.regex})" for p in self._patterns)
        self._compiled = re.compile(source, flags)

    @staticmethod
    def _validate(patterns: Sequence[TokenPattern]) -> None:
        seen = set()
        for pattern in patterns:
            if not _NAME_RE.match(pattern.name):
                raise ValueError(f"invalid pattern name: {pattern.name!r}")
            if pattern.name in seen:
                raise ValueError(f"duplicate pattern name: {pattern.name!r}")
            seen.add(pattern.name)
            try:
                compiled = re.compile(pattern.regex)
            except re.error as exc:
                raise ValueError(f"bad regex for {pattern.name}: {exc}") from exc
            if compiled.groupindex:
                raise ValueError(f"pattern {pattern.name} must not define named groups")
            if compiled.match(""):
                raise ValueError(f"pattern {pattern.name} must not match empty text")

    @property
    def pattern_names(self) -> List[str]:
        """Pattern names in priority order."""
        return [p.name for p in self._patterns]

    def tokenize(self, text: str) -> Iterator[Token]:
        """Yield tokens lazily, left to right."""
        position = 0
        length = len(text)
        while position < length:
            match = self._compiled.match(text, position)
            if match is None:
                if self._on_error == "raise":
                    raise TokenizeError(text, position)
                if self._on_error == "emit":
                    yield Token("UNKNOWN", text[position], position, position + 1)
                position += 1
                continue
            name = match.lastgroup
            if name not in self._skip:
                yield Token(name, match.group(), match.start(), match.end())
            position = match.end()

    def tokens(self, text: str) -> List[Token]:
        """Return all tokens for text as a list."""
        return list(self.tokenize(text))

    def split(self, text: str) -> List[str]:
        """Return only the token strings, without type information."""
        return [token.text for token in self.tokenize(text)]

title: tokenizers/sentence.py — Sentence boundary detection with abbreviation handling
text:
tokenizers/sentence.py — Sentence boundary detection with abbreviation handling

```python
"""Sentence boundary detection with abbreviation handling.

The splitter looks for runs of terminal punctuation followed by whitespace
and then decides, one candidate at a time, whether the punctuation really
ends a sentence. The decision uses only local context: the word before the
punctuation and the first character after the whitespace.

Rules, applied in order:

1. "!" or "?" in the run always ends a sentence.
2. A run of several periods (an ellipsis) ends a sentence unless the next
   character is lowercase.
3. A single period after a title abbreviation ("Dr.", "Mr.") never ends one.
4. A single period after a lone capital letter (an initial) never ends one.
5. A single period after another known abbreviation ends a sentence only
   if the next character is uppercase.
6. Any other single period ends a sentence unless the next character is
   lowercase.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import re
from typing import Iterable, Iterator, List, Optional

# Abbreviations that are almost always followed by a name or a number, so
# the period after them is never treated as a sentence end.
TITLE_ABBREVIATIONS = frozenset({
    "mr", "mrs", "ms", "dr", "prof", "sr", "jr", "st", "mt",
    "gen", "col", "capt", "lt", "sgt", "rev", "hon", "vs",
})

# Abbreviations that may legitimately appear at the end of a sentence.
GENERAL_ABBREVIATIONS = frozenset({
    "etc", "inc", "ltd", "co", "corp", "approx", "dept", "est",
    "e.g", "i.e", "u.s", "u.k", "a.m", "p.m", "no", "fig", "vol",
})

_CANDIDATE = re.compile(r"([.!?]+)([\"')\]}\u201d\u2019]*)(\s+)")
_INITIAL = re.compile(r"[A-Z]")
_OPENERS = "\"'([{\u201c\u2018"


class SentenceSplitter:
    """Split text into sentences using punctuation and abbreviation lists.

    Parameters
    ----------
    titles:
        Lowercase abbreviations (without the final period) that never end
        a sentence. Defaults to ``TITLE_ABBREVIATIONS``.
    abbreviations:
        Lowercase abbreviations that may end a sentence when followed by
        an uppercase letter. Defaults to ``GENERAL_ABBREVIATIONS``.
    extra:
        Additional abbreviations to add to ``abbreviations``.
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        titles: Optional[Iterable[str]] = None,
        abbreviations: Optional[Iterable[str]] = None,
        extra: Iterable[str] = (),
    ) -> None:
        self.titles = frozenset(
            TITLE_ABBREVIATIONS if titles is None else titles
        )
        base = GENERAL_ABBREVIATIONS if abbreviations is None else abbreviations
        self.abbreviations = frozenset(base) | frozenset(
            item.lower().rstrip(".") for item in extra
        )

    @staticmethod
    def _previous_word(text: str, end: int) -> str:
        """Return the whitespace-delimited word that finishes at ``end``."""
        start = end
        while start > 0 and not text[start - 1].isspace():
            start -= 1
        return text[start:end]

    def _is_boundary(self, text: str, match: "re.Match[str]") -> bool:
        """Decide whether the punctuation run in ``match`` ends a sentence."""
        marks = match.group(1)
        following = text[match.end():][:1]
        if not following:
            return True
        if "!" in marks or "?" in marks:
            return True
        if len(marks) > 1:
            return not following.islower()

        word = self._previous_word(text, match.start()).lstrip(_OPENERS)
        key = word.lower()
        if key in self.titles:
            return False
        if _INITIAL.fullmatch(word):
            return False
        if key in self.abbreviations:
            return following.isupper()
        return not following.islower()

    def iter_sentences(self, text: str) -> Iterator[str]:
        """Yield sentences one at a time, with surrounding space removed."""
        start = 0
        for match in _CANDIDATE.finditer(text):
            if not self._is_boundary(text, match):
                continue
            sentence = text[start:match.end(2)].strip()
            if sentence:
                yield sentence
            start = match.end()
        tail = text[start:].strip()
        if tail:
            yield tail

    def split(self, text: str) -> List[str]:
        """Return all sentences in ``text`` as a list."""
        return list(self.iter_sentences(text))


_default_splitter = SentenceSplitter()


def split_sentences(text: str, splitter: Optional[SentenceSplitter] = None) -> List[str]:
    """Split ``text`` into sentences with the default or a supplied splitter."""
    return (splitter or _default_splitter).split(text)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sample = "Dr. Smith met J. Doe at 5 p.m. They talked. Was it useful? Yes!"
    for item in split_sentences(sample):
        print(item)
```

title: tokenizers/ngrams.py — Generate character and word n-grams from token streams
text:
tokenizers/ngrams.py — Generate character and word n-grams from token streams

```python
"""N-gram generation for the tokenizers package.

This module produces contiguous n-grams from two kinds of input:

* a string, yielding character n-grams (``char_ngrams``)
* an iterable of tokens, yielding word n-grams (``word_ngrams``)

Word n-gram generation is lazy. Tokens are consumed one at a time and only
a window of the most recent ``n`` tokens is held in memory, so the functions
can be used on very large streams, such as tokens read line by line from a
file.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from collections import Counter, deque
from itertools import chain, repeat
from typing import Hashable, Iterable, Iterator, Optional, Tuple

__all__ = [
    "char_ngrams",
    "word_ngrams",
    "ngram_range",
    "count_ngrams",
]


def _check_n(n: int, name: str = "n") -> None:
    """Raise if ``n`` is not a positive integer."""
    if isinstance(n, bool) or not isinstance(n, int):
        raise TypeError(f"{name} must be an int, got {type(n).__name__}")
    if n < 1:
        raise ValueError(f"{name} must be at least 1, got {n}")


def char_ngrams(text: str, n: int, pad: Optional[str] = None) -> Iterator[str]:
    """Yield character n-grams of ``text`` in order of appearance.

    Args:
        text: The input string.
        n: Length of each n-gram.
        pad: Optional padding character. When given, ``n - 1`` copies are
            added to both ends so that the first and last characters
            appear in as many n-grams as interior characters do.

    Strings shorter than ``n`` yield nothing.

    >>> list(char_ngrams("abcd", 2))
    ['ab', 'bc', 'cd']
    >>> list(char_ngrams("ab", 2, pad="_"))
    ['_a', 'ab', 'b_']
    """
    _check_n(n)
    if pad is not None:
        if len(pad) != 1:
            raise ValueError("pad must be a single character")
        edge = pad * (n - 1)
        text = edge + text + edge
    for start in range(len(text) - n + 1):
        yield text[start:start + n]


def word_ngrams(
    tokens: Iterable[str],
    n: int,
    pad: Optional[str] = None,
    sep: Optional[str] = None,
) -> Iterator[Tuple[str, ...] | str]:
    """Yield word n-grams from a stream of tokens.

    Args:
        tokens: Any iterable of tokens. It is consumed lazily and only once.
        n: Number of tokens in each n-gram.
        pad: Optional padding token. When given, ``n - 1`` copies are
            emitted before the first token and after the last one.
        sep: If given, each n-gram is joined into a single string using
            this separator. Otherwise a tuple of tokens is yielded.

    >>> list(word_ngrams(["a", "b", "c"], 2))
    [('a', 'b'), ('b', 'c')]
    >>> list(word_ngrams(["a", "b", "c"], 2, sep=" "))
    ['a b', 'b c']
    """
    _check_n(n)
    stream: Iterable[str] = tokens
    if pad is not None:
        edge = repeat(pad, n - 1)
        stream = chain(edge, tokens, repeat(pad, n - 1))

    window: deque = deque(maxlen=n)
    for token in stream:
        window.append(token)
        if len(window) == n:
            yield sep.join(window) if sep is not None else tuple(window)


def ngram_range(
    tokens: Iterable[str],
    min_n: int,
    max_n: int,
    sep: str = " ",
) -> Iterator[str]:
    """Yield joined word n-grams for every size from ``min_n`` to ``max_n``.

    The token stream is materialised once, because several passes over it
    are required. Output is grouped by n-gram size, smallest size first.

    >>> list(ngram_range(["a", "b", "c"], 1, 2))
    ['a', 'b', 'c', 'a b', 'b c']
    """
    _check_n(min_n, "min_n")
    _check_n(max_n, "max_n")
    if min_n > max_n:
        raise ValueError("min_n must not be greater than max_n")

    items = list(tokens)
    for size in range(min_n, max_n + 1):
        yield from word_ngrams(items, size, sep=sep)


def count_ngrams(ngrams: Iterable[Hashable]) -> "Counter[Hashable]":
    """Count how often each n-gram occurs.

    Works with the output of any function in this module, whether the
    n-grams are strings or tuples.

    >>> count_ngrams(word_ngrams(["a", "b", "a", "b"], 2, sep=" "))
    Counter({'a b': 2, 'b a': 1})
    """
    return Counter(ngrams)
```

title: tokenizers/code_aware.py — Tokenize identifiers in camelCase, snake_case and kebab-case
text:
tokenizers/code_aware.py — Tokenize identifiers in camelCase, snake_case and kebab-case

```python
"""Code-aware tokenization.

General-purpose tokenizers treat an identifier such as ``parseHTTPResponse``
or ``max_retry-count`` as a single opaque word. This module splits such
identifiers into their natural sub-words so that search, indexing and
similarity features can match ``parse`` or ``response`` inside them.

Supported conventions:

* camelCase and PascalCase    -> ``getUserName``     -> get, user, name
* acronym runs                -> ``parseHTTPResponse`` -> parse, http, response
* snake_case / SCREAMING_CASE -> ``MAX_RETRY_COUNT`` -> max, retry, count
* kebab-case                  -> ``main-nav-item``   -> main, nav, item
* mixed conventions           -> ``my_fooBar-baz``   -> my, foo, bar, baz
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import re
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Iterable, Iterator, List

__all__ = ["split_identifier", "CodeAwareTokenizer"]

# An identifier starts with a letter or underscore and may contain letters,
# digits and underscores. Hyphen-joined groups are accepted so that
# kebab-case names are matched as one candidate.
_IDENTIFIER_RE = re.compile(r"[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*(?:-[A-Za-z0-9_]+)*")

# Runs of explicit separators between sub-words.
_SEPARATOR_RE = re.compile(r"[_\-]+")

# Zero-width positions at which a camelCase chunk is divided:
#   1. a lowercase letter or digit followed by an uppercase letter
#      (``userName`` -> ``user|Name``)
#   2. the last capital of an acronym followed by a capitalised word
#      (``HTTPResponse`` -> ``HTTP|Response``)
_CAMEL_BOUNDARY_RE = re.compile(
    r"(?<=[a-z0-9])(?=[A-Z])|(?<=[A-Z])(?=[A-Z][a-z])"
)

# Zero-width positions between a letter and a digit, in either order.
_DIGIT_BOUNDARY_RE = re.compile(r"(?<=[A-Za-z])(?=[0-9])|(?<=[0-9])(?=[A-Za-z])")


def split_identifier(
    identifier: str,
    *,
    lowercase: bool = True,
    split_digits: bool = False,
) -> List[str]:
    """Split a single identifier into its sub-words.

    Args:
        identifier: The identifier to split, in any supported convention.
        lowercase: Convert every sub-word to lower case.
        split_digits: Also separate digit runs from adjacent letters, so
            ``sha256sum`` becomes ``sha``, ``256``, ``sum``.

    Returns:
        The sub-words in their original order. An identifier that contains
        only separators yields an empty list.
    """
    words: List[str] = []
    for chunk in _SEPARATOR_RE.split(identifier):
        if not chunk:
            continue
        for piece in _CAMEL_BOUNDARY_RE.split(chunk):
            parts = _DIGIT_BOUNDARY_RE.split(piece) if split_digits else [piece]
            for part in parts:
                if part:
                    words.append(part.lower() if lowercase else part)
    return words


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CodeAwareTokenizer:
    """Tokenizer that extracts identifiers from text and splits them.

    Attributes:
        lowercase: Convert sub-words to lower case.
        split_digits: Separate digit runs from adjacent letters.
        min_length: Sub-words shorter than this are discarded.
        keep_original: Emit the full identifier before its sub-words
            whenever the identifier was actually divided. This helps
            exact-match lookups while still allowing partial matches.
    """

    lowercase: bool = True
    split_digits: bool = False
    min_length: int = 1
    keep_original: bool = False

    def iter_tokens(self, text: str) -> Iterator[str]:
        """Yield tokens lazily from ``text``."""
        for match in _IDENTIFIER_RE.finditer(text):
            identifier = match.group(0)
            words = split_identifier(
                identifier,
                lowercase=self.lowercase,
                split_digits=self.split_digits,
            )
            words = [w for w in words if len(w) >= self.min_length]
            if self.keep_original and len(words) > 1:
                yield identifier.lower() if self.lowercase else identifier
            yield from words

    def tokenize(self, text: str) -> List[str]:
        """Return all tokens found in ``text`` as a list."""
        return list(self.iter_tokens(text))

    def tokenize_many(self, texts: Iterable[str]) -> List[List[str]]:
        """Tokenize each string in ``texts`` independently."""
        return [self.tokenize(text) for text in texts]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    demo = CodeAwareTokenizer(keep_original=True)
    print(demo.tokenize("def parseHTTPResponse(max_retry_count, main-nav):"))
```

title: tokenizers/emoji.py — Detect and isolate emoji and pictographs as separate tokens
text:
tokenizers/emoji.py — Detect and isolate emoji and pictographs as separate tokens

```python
"""Emoji-aware tokenization.

Splits a string into alternating runs of ordinary text and emoji sequences.
A single emoji token may span several code points: a base pictograph with a
variation selector or skin-tone modifier, a zero-width-joiner (ZWJ) family,
a pair of regional indicators (a flag), a keycap, or a tag sequence.

No third-party data is required. Detection uses a compact table of code point
ranges that covers the blocks in common use.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Iterator, List

ZWJ = "\u200d"
VS16 = "\ufe0f"          # requests emoji presentation
KEYCAP = "\u20e3"        # combining enclosing keycap
_KEYCAP_BASES = frozenset("0123456789#*")

# Ranges whose members are rendered as emoji by default.
_EMOJI_DEFAULT_RANGES = (
    (0x1F300, 0x1F5FF),  # symbols and pictographs
    (0x1F600, 0x1F64F),  # emoticons
    (0x1F680, 0x1F6FF),  # transport and map symbols
    (0x1F900, 0x1F9FF),  # supplemental symbols and pictographs
    (0x1FA70, 0x1FAFF),  # extended pictographs
    (0x1F1E6, 0x1F1FF),  # regional indicators (handled separately)
)

# Symbols that look like text unless followed by VS16, so a bare
# occurrence is left as ordinary text.
_TEXT_DEFAULT_RANGES = (
    (0x2190, 0x21FF),    # arrows
    (0x2600, 0x26FF),    # miscellaneous symbols
    (0x2700, 0x27BF),    # dingbats
)
_TEXT_DEFAULT_SINGLES = frozenset(
    [0x00A9, 0x00AE, 0x203C, 0x2049, 0x2122, 0x2139, 0x3030, 0x303D]
)

_SKIN_TONE_RANGE = (0x1F3FB, 0x1F3FF)
_TAG_RANGE = (0xE0020, 0xE007F)
_REGIONAL_RANGE = (0x1F1E6, 0x1F1FF)


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class EmojiToken:
    """A slice of the source string, classified as emoji or plain text."""

    text: str
    start: int
    end: int
    is_emoji: bool


def _within(cp: int, bounds: tuple) -> bool:
    return bounds[0] <= cp <= bounds[1]


def _in_any(cp: int, ranges) -> bool:
    return any(lo <= cp <= hi for lo, hi in ranges)


def _is_default_emoji(ch: str) -> bool:
    return _in_any(ord(ch), _EMOJI_DEFAULT_RANGES)


def _is_text_default(ch: str) -> bool:
    cp = ord(ch)
    return cp in _TEXT_DEFAULT_SINGLES or _in_any(cp, _TEXT_DEFAULT_RANGES)


def _emoji_end(text: str, i: int) -> int:
    """Return the index just past an emoji sequence starting at ``i``.

    The result equals ``i`` when no emoji sequence begins there.
    """
    n = len(text)
    ch = text[i]
    cp = ord(ch)

    # Keycap: digit, '#' or '*', optional VS16, then the keycap mark.
    if ch in _KEYCAP_BASES:
        j = i + 1
        if j < n and text[j] == VS16:
            j += 1
        if j < n and text[j] == KEYCAP:
            return j + 1
        return i

    # Flag: two regional indicators form one token. A lone indicator
    # is still reported as emoji so that it is not merged into text.
    if _within(cp, _REGIONAL_RANGE):
        j = i + 1
        if j < n and _within(ord(text[j]), _REGIONAL_RANGE):
            return j + 1
        return j

    if _is_default_emoji(ch):
        j = i + 1
    elif _is_text_default(ch) and i + 1 < n and text[i + 1] == VS16:
        j = i + 1
    else:
        return i

    # Absorb modifiers, selectors, tag characters and joined elements.
    while j < n:
        c = text[j]
        c_cp = ord(c)
        if c == VS16 or _within(c_cp, _SKIN_TONE_RANGE) or _within(c_cp, _TAG_RANGE):
            j += 1
        elif c == ZWJ and j + 1 < n and (
            _is_default_emoji(text[j + 1]) or _is_text_default(text[j + 1])
        ):
            # Continue the sequence with the element after the joiner.
            j += 2
        else:
            break
    return j


def tokenize_emoji(text: str, keep_text: bool = True) -> Iterator[EmojiToken]:
    """Yield tokens covering ``text`` in order.

    Emoji sequences become tokens with ``is_emoji=True``. Text between them
    is yielded as a single token with ``is_emoji=False`` unless ``keep_text``
    is false, in which case only emoji tokens are produced.
    """
    n = len(text)
    i = 0
    run_start = 0
    while i < n:
        end = _emoji_end(text, i)
        if end == i:
            i += 1
            continue
        if keep_text and run_start < i:
            yield EmojiToken(text[run_start:i], run_start, i, False)
        yield EmojiToken(text[i:end], i, end, True)
        i = end
        run_start = end
    if keep_text and run_start < n:
        yield EmojiToken(text[run_start:n], run_start, n, False)


def extract_emoji(text: str) -> List[str]:
    """Return every emoji sequence found in ``text``, in order."""
    return [t.text for t in tokenize_emoji(text, keep_text=False)]


def count_emoji(text: str) -> int:
    """Return the number of emoji sequences in ``text``."""
    return sum(1 for _ in tokenize_emoji(text, keep_text=False))


def strip_emoji(text: str) -> str:
    """Return ``text`` with all emoji sequences removed."""
    return "".join(t.text for t in tokenize_emoji(text) if not t.is_emoji)
```
audit_reason: The code contains arithmetic: index offsets such as i + 1, j + 2 and j += 2, plus count_emoji computing a total with sum(1 for ...), and the ranges and code points are literal constants rather than derived values.

title: tokenizers/stream.py — Lazy generator-based tokenization for large inputs
text:
tokenizers/stream.py — Lazy generator-based tokenization for large inputs

```python
"""Lazy, generator-based tokenization for large inputs.

The functions in this module read text in fixed-size chunks and yield
tokens one at a time, so memory use depends on the chunk size and the
longest token rather than on the size of the input.

Chunk boundaries are handled by holding back any trailing partial word
until the next chunk arrives, so a token is never split in two.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import re
from dataclasses import dataclass
from itertools import islice
from typing import IO, Iterable, Iterator, List, Optional, Union

DEFAULT_CHUNK_SIZE = 65536

# A token is either a word (letters, digits, underscores, with optional
# internal apostrophes or hyphens) or a single punctuation character.
DEFAULT_PATTERN = re.compile(r"\w+(?:['\u2019-]\w+)*|[^\w\s]")

Source = Union[str, IO[str], Iterable[str]]


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Token:
    """A token together with its character offset in the whole input."""

    text: str
    offset: int

    def __str__(self) -> str:
        return self.text


def iter_chunks(source: Source, chunk_size: int = DEFAULT_CHUNK_SIZE) -> Iterator[str]:
    """Yield the contents of *source* as a sequence of strings.

    *source* may be a plain string, a text file object, or any iterable
    of strings (for example a list of lines or another generator).
    """
    if chunk_size <= 0:
        raise ValueError("chunk_size must be a positive integer")

    if isinstance(source, str):
        for start in range(0, len(source), chunk_size):
            yield source[start:start + chunk_size]
    elif hasattr(source, "read"):
        while True:
            chunk = source.read(chunk_size)
            if not chunk:
                break
            yield chunk
    else:
        for piece in source:
            if piece:
                yield piece


def _safe_split_point(buffer: str) -> int:
    """Return the index just after the last whitespace character.

    Text before the returned index is guaranteed to end on a token
    boundary. Zero means the buffer holds no whitespace and must be
    extended before it can be tokenized safely.
    """
    index = len(buffer)
    while index > 0 and not buffer[index - 1].isspace():
        index -= 1
    return index


def stream_tokens(
    source: Source,
    pattern: Optional[re.Pattern] = None,
    chunk_size: int = DEFAULT_CHUNK_SIZE,
    lowercase: bool = False,
) -> Iterator[Token]:
    """Lazily yield :class:`Token` objects from *source*.

    Offsets are character positions relative to the start of the entire
    input, not to the current chunk.
    """
    regex = pattern or DEFAULT_PATTERN
    carry = ""
    base = 0  # offset of carry[0] within the whole input

    for chunk in iter_chunks(source, chunk_size):
        buffer = carry + chunk
        split = _safe_split_point(buffer)
        if split == 0:
            # No boundary yet; keep accumulating.
            carry = buffer
            continue

        for match in regex.finditer(buffer, 0, split):
            text = match.group()
            yield Token(text.lower() if lowercase else text, base + match.start())

        base += split
        carry = buffer[split:]

    # Whatever remains after the final chunk is complete by definition.
    for match in regex.finditer(carry):
        text = match.group()
        yield Token(text.lower() if lowercase else text, base + match.start())


def stream_words(source: Source, **options) -> Iterator[str]:
    """Yield plain token strings, discarding offsets."""
    for token in stream_tokens(source, **options):
        yield token.text


def stream_file(path: str, encoding: str = "utf-8", **options) -> Iterator[Token]:
    """Open *path* and lazily tokenize it.

    The file stays open only while the generator is being consumed and
    is closed when the generator is exhausted or garbage collected.
    """
    with open(path, "r", encoding=encoding) as handle:
        yield from stream_tokens(handle, **options)


def batched_tokens(tokens: Iterable[Token], size: int) -> Iterator[List[Token]]:
    """Group a token stream into lists of at most *size* tokens."""
    if size <= 0:
        raise ValueError("size must be a positive integer")
    iterator = iter(tokens)
    while True:
        batch = list(islice(iterator, size))
        if not batch:
            return
        yield batch
```
audit_reason: The code computes running offsets: `base += split` and `base + match.start()` add numbers derived from other values, and `index -= 1` decrements an index, so it contains arithmetic; the prose and comments are plain technical description with no mocking or sarcastic tone.

title: cleaning/whitespace.py — Collapse, trim and normalize spaces, tabs and newlines
text:
cleaning/whitespace.py — Collapse, trim and normalize spaces, tabs and newlines

```python
"""Whitespace helpers for the cleaning package.

The functions here operate on plain ``str`` objects and never modify their
input. Each one does a single job, and ``normalize_whitespace`` combines them
in a sensible order for the common case of preparing text for tokenising.

Terminology used in this module:

* horizontal whitespace: spaces, tabs and other blanks that do not end a line
* line break: any sequence that separates lines (``\\n``, ``\\r\\n``, ``\\r``, and
  the Unicode line and paragraph separators)
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import re
import unicodedata
from typing import Iterable, Iterator

__all__ = [
    "normalize_newlines",
    "replace_unicode_spaces",
    "collapse_spaces",
    "strip_lines",
    "collapse_blank_lines",
    "normalize_whitespace",
]

# Any single character that counts as whitespace but is not a line break.
_HORIZONTAL_RUN = re.compile(r"[^\S\r\n]+")

# Line break variants that are rewritten to a plain newline. The two-character
# sequence must come first so that it is not split into two breaks.
_LINE_BREAKS = re.compile("\r\n|\r|\u2028|\u2029|\x0b|\x0c|\x85")

# Zero-width characters that render as nothing but still affect comparisons.
_INVISIBLES = dict.fromkeys(map(ord, "\u200b\u200c\u200d\u2060\ufeff"))


def normalize_newlines(text: str, newline: str = "\n") -> str:
    """Rewrite every line break variant in ``text`` as ``newline``.

    >>> normalize_newlines("a\\r\\nb\\rc")
    'a\\nb\\nc'
    """
    return _LINE_BREAKS.sub(newline, text)


def replace_unicode_spaces(text: str, remove_invisible: bool = True) -> str:
    """Turn exotic space characters into ordinary spaces.

    Characters in the Unicode "Zs" category (no-break space, thin space,
    ideographic space and so on) become a plain space. When
    ``remove_invisible`` is true, zero-width characters and byte order marks
    are deleted instead of being replaced.
    """
    if remove_invisible:
        text = text.translate(_INVISIBLES)
    return "".join(
        " " if unicodedata.category(ch) == "Zs" else ch for ch in text
    )


def collapse_spaces(text: str, replacement: str = " ") -> str:
    """Replace each run of horizontal whitespace with ``replacement``.

    Line breaks are left untouched, so the line structure of the text is
    preserved. A single tab is replaced as well, not only runs of several
    characters.

    >>> collapse_spaces("a \\t  b\\nc\\t\\td")
    'a b\\nc d'
    """
    return _HORIZONTAL_RUN.sub(replacement, text)


def strip_lines(text: str, *, left: bool = True, right: bool = True) -> str:
    """Strip horizontal whitespace from the edges of every line.

    ``left`` and ``right`` choose which side is trimmed. The number of lines
    in the result always matches the number of lines in the input.
    """
    lines = _split_lines(text)
    if left and right:
        cleaned = (line.strip() for line in lines)
    elif left:
        cleaned = (line.lstrip() for line in lines)
    elif right:
        cleaned = (line.rstrip() for line in lines)
    else:
        return text
    return "\n".join(cleaned)


def collapse_blank_lines(text: str, max_blank: int = 1) -> str:
    """Limit consecutive empty lines to ``max_blank``.

    A line that contains only whitespace is treated as empty. With
    ``max_blank=0`` all empty lines are removed.

    Raises ``ValueError`` if ``max_blank`` is negative.
    """
    if max_blank < 0:
        raise ValueError("max_blank must not be negative")

    kept: list[str] = []
    run_length = 0
    for line in _split_lines(text):
        if line.strip():
            run_length = 0
            kept.append(line)
            continue
        if run_length < max_blank:
            kept.append("")
        run_length += 1
    return "\n".join(kept)


def normalize_whitespace(
    text: str,
    *,
    keep_newlines: bool = True,
    max_blank_lines: int = 1,
    tab_size: int | None = None,
) -> str:
    """Apply the standard whitespace cleanup pipeline.

    Steps, in order:

    1. unify line breaks
    2. replace Unicode spaces and drop invisible characters
    3. optionally expand tabs to ``tab_size`` columns
    4. collapse horizontal runs and trim each line
    5. limit blank lines, then trim the whole text

    With ``keep_newlines=False`` the result is a single line in which every
    run of whitespace, line breaks included, is one space.
    """
    text = normalize_newlines(text)
    text = replace_unicode_spaces(text)
    if tab_size is not None:
        text = text.expandtabs(tab_size)

    if not keep_newlines:
        return " ".join(text.split())

    text = collapse_spaces(text)
    text = strip_lines(text)
    text = collapse_blank_lines(text, max_blank_lines)
    return text.strip("\n")


def _split_lines(text: str) -> list[str]:
    """Split on newlines only, keeping a trailing empty string if present."""
    return text.split("\n")


def iter_clean_lines(lines: Iterable[str]) -> Iterator[str]:
    """Yield non-empty lines with surrounding whitespace removed.

    Useful for streaming input where the full text is never held in memory.
    """
    for line in lines:
        stripped = line.strip()
        if stripped:
            yield stripped
```

title: cleaning/unicode_normalize.py — NFC/NFD/NFKC normalization helpers
text:
cleaning/unicode_normalize.py — NFC/NFD/NFKC normalization helpers

```python
"""Unicode normalization helpers.

The same visible text can be stored as different code point sequences. For
example, "é" may be one precomposed code point or an "e" followed by a
combining acute accent. Comparing, hashing, or indexing such strings without
normalizing them first gives inconsistent results.

This module wraps :mod:`unicodedata` with input validation and a few
conveniences used elsewhere in the cleaning package:

* NFC  - canonical composition (the usual choice for storage and display)
* NFD  - canonical decomposition (useful before removing accents)
* NFKC - compatibility composition (folds ligatures, full-width forms, etc.)
* NFKD - compatibility decomposition
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import unicodedata
from typing import Dict, Iterable, Iterator, List, Tuple

__all__ = [
    "NormalizationError",
    "Normalizer",
    "normalize",
    "to_nfc",
    "to_nfd",
    "to_nfkc",
    "to_nfkd",
    "is_normalized",
    "strip_combining",
    "equivalent",
    "normalize_lines",
    "normalize_keys",
    "find_unnormalized",
]

VALID_FORMS = frozenset({"NFC", "NFD", "NFKC", "NFKD"})


class NormalizationError(ValueError):
    """Raised for an unknown form name or a key collision after normalizing."""


def _check_form(form: str) -> str:
    """Return the upper-case form name or raise NormalizationError."""
    name = str(form).upper()
    if name not in VALID_FORMS:
        allowed = ", ".join(sorted(VALID_FORMS))
        raise NormalizationError(f"unknown form {form!r}; expected one of: {allowed}")
    return name


def normalize(text: str, form: str = "NFC") -> str:
    """Normalize ``text`` to the requested Unicode form (default NFC)."""
    return unicodedata.normalize(_check_form(form), text)


def to_nfc(text: str) -> str:
    return normalize(text, "NFC")


def to_nfd(text: str) -> str:
    return normalize(text, "NFD")


def to_nfkc(text: str) -> str:
    """Compatibility composition; may change meaning-adjacent characters."""
    return normalize(text, "NFKC")


def to_nfkd(text: str) -> str:
    return normalize(text, "NFKD")


def is_normalized(text: str, form: str = "NFC") -> bool:
    """Return True if ``text`` is already in the given form."""
    return unicodedata.is_normalized(_check_form(form), text)


def strip_combining(text: str) -> str:
    """Remove combining marks, e.g. turn "café" into "cafe".

    The text is decomposed, combining characters are dropped, and the
    result is recomposed so that remaining characters are in NFC.
    """
    decomposed = unicodedata.normalize("NFD", text)
    kept = "".join(ch for ch in decomposed if not unicodedata.combining(ch))
    return unicodedata.normalize("NFC", kept)


def equivalent(a: str, b: str, form: str = "NFC", casefold: bool = False) -> bool:
    """Compare two strings after normalization.

    With ``casefold=True`` the comparison is also case-insensitive. Case
    folding can produce text that is no longer normalized, so the strings
    are normalized again afterwards.
    """
    left, right = normalize(a, form), normalize(b, form)
    if casefold:
        left = normalize(left.casefold(), form)
        right = normalize(right.casefold(), form)
    return left == right


def normalize_lines(lines: Iterable[str], form: str = "NFC") -> Iterator[str]:
    """Lazily normalize each string in ``lines``.

    Line endings are preserved because normalization does not touch them.
    """
    name = _check_form(form)
    for line in lines:
        yield unicodedata.normalize(name, line)


def normalize_keys(mapping: Dict[str, object], form: str = "NFC") -> Dict[str, object]:
    """Return a copy of ``mapping`` with all keys normalized.

    Two keys that differ only in normalization would silently overwrite each
    other, so a NormalizationError is raised instead.
    """
    name = _check_form(form)
    result: Dict[str, object] = {}
    for key, value in mapping.items():
        new_key = unicodedata.normalize(name, key)
        if new_key in result:
            raise NormalizationError(f"keys collide after {name}: {new_key!r}")
        result[new_key] = value
    return result


def find_unnormalized(text: str, form: str = "NFC") -> List[Tuple[int, str]]:
    """Report characters that would change under ``form``.

    Each character is checked on its own, so sequences that only change in
    combination (such as a base letter followed by a combining mark) are
    not reported individually. Use :func:`is_normalized` for a definitive
    answer about the whole string.
    """
    name = _check_form(form)
    return [
        (index, ch)
        for index, ch in enumerate(text)
        if not unicodedata.is_normalized(name, ch)
    ]


class Normalizer:
    """Reusable, configurable normalization step.

    >>> clean = Normalizer(form="NFKC", casefold=True)
    >>> clean("ＡＢＣ")
    'abc'
    """

    def __init__(self, form: str = "NFC", casefold: bool = False,
                 drop_accents: bool = False) -> None:
        self.form = _check_form(form)
        self.casefold = casefold
        self.drop_accents = drop_accents

    def __call__(self, text: str) -> str:
        out = unicodedata.normalize(self.form, text)
        if self.drop_accents:
            out = strip_combining(out)
        if self.casefold:
            out = out.casefold()
        # Accent removal and case folding can leave the text unnormalized.
        return unicodedata.normalize(self.form, out)

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        return (f"Normalizer(form={self.form!r}, casefold={self.casefold}, "
                f"drop_accents={self.drop_accents})")
```
